catalogTitle: משה רבינו מלמד איך להתפלל. נחיצות וחשיבות פסוקי דזמרה

oneLiner.en: From Parshas Va'eschanan the Rav shows that Moshe Rabbeinu teaches how to daven, and explains why pesukei dezimra, the songs of David Hamelech that cut a path for tefillah, are so precious precisely because they are less obligatory.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the season of tefillah that begins now and runs until Shemini Atzeres, and with Moshe Rabbeinu's many prayers to enter the land and see the Beis Hamikdash, the house of prayer. Moshe teaches that one first sets out the praise of Hashem and only then prays. Davening has three stages: korbanos, pesukei dezimra and the contemplative tefillah. Like an army breaking through enemy lines, korbanos and the songs of David, the warrior king, cut through the forces that block prayer. The Rav laments that many skip pesukei dezimra as a lesser obligation, and answers that the less obligatory a thing is, the dearer it is, as with Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair. He speaks of saying the praises together, of Hallel Hagadol and Nishmas on Shabbos, of davening with the tzibbur on time and with warmth, and closes with stories of the Rebbe Reb Elimelech and a call to use every minute in camp.

en: Moshe Rabbeinu's prayers in Va'eschanan teach that one first sets out the praise of Hashem and only afterwards prays.
Korbanos and pesukei dezimra cut a path through the forces that block tefillah, like an army breaking through enemy positions.
Pesukei dezimra is not a lesser part of davening: the less obligatory a thing is, the dearer it is to Hashem.
One should daven together with the tzibbur, come on time and keep pace with the chazzan, and one owes the tzibbur a lively davening that arouses others.
Tefillah requires toil just as Torah does; davening with warmth and a raised voice breaks through the coarseness of the body.
The 'uncle' who talks a Jew out of a good deed is the yetzer hara in disguise, and one must recognize him.

title.en: The season of tefillah and Moshe's prayers

summary.en: The Rav opens with the parsha's teaching on tefillah and the period that leads to Rosh Hashanah and Shemini Atzeres. He connects the Beis Hamikdash, the house of prayer, with Moshe Rabbeinu's longing to enter the land, and says Moshe now teaches how to daven.

title.en: Three stages of davening: cutting a path

summary.en: The Rav lays out three kinds of prayer, the tefillah of Moshe, of the poor man and of David, and three stages of davening. Like an army breaking through enemy lines, korbanos and pesukei dezimra, the songs of David the warrior, cut through the forces that block prayer, just as the shofar does on Rosh Hashanah; the lesson from Moshe is to praise the King before asking.

title.en: Why pesukei dezimra is not taken lightly

summary.en: The Rav laments that even bnei Torah treat pesukei dezimra as minor because it is less obligatory than the blessings of Shema. He answers that the less obligatory a thing is, the more precious it is, like a gift beyond the bread one must provide, and notes that pesukei dezimra come from David Hamelech himself.

title.en: Hiddur and Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair

summary.en: The Rav explains that the hiddur of a mitzvah gives Hashem more pleasure than the bare mitzvah, and brings the Gemara about Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and the river Ginai: self-sacrifice for a doubtful mitzvah shows greater devotion than for a certain one. So too pesukei dezimra, less obligatory, is dearer.

title.en: Singing together; Shabbos and Hallel Hagadol

summary.en: The Rav says the praises should be said together, as the angels sing in unison. On Shabbos more chapters are added because Shabbos lifts the tefillos of the week, and in Hallel Hagadol each angel can say only one praise while a Jew says them all.

title.en: Nishmas and the Sassover Rebbe

summary.en: The Rav describes how earlier generations waited all week for Nishmas, where the extra soul of Shabbos morning is received. He tells how Rebbe Moshe Leib of Sassov, starving at a poritz's feast during a mission of pidyon shvuyim, forgot his hunger by thinking of saying Nishmas.

title.en: Shabbos is all song; Moshe in every shul

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the weekday alphabetic blessing, a word per letter, with Shabbos's 'Kel Adon', a phrase per letter, because Shabbos's added holiness is all song. He urges davening together near the shliach tzibbur and says that when the parsha is read, Moshe Rabbeinu comes to every shul to teach how to daven.

title.en: Davening with the tzibbur, on time

summary.en: The Rav asks that people come on time and daven together like one orchestra, keeping pace with the chazzan. He explains that the chassidic custom of davening later on Shabbos came from learning before davening, not from sleeping late.

title.en: What one owes the tzibbur; Torah with tefillah

summary.en: The Rav says each person is part of the congregation and owes it a lively davening that inspires others. He speaks of Shabbos as a day for Torah, of Torah and tefillah needing each other, of strengthening Torah study as the nights lengthen before the Yamim Noraim, and of this Shabbos as a time to take on tefillah.

title.en: Why a Jew comes to a place

summary.en: The Rav teaches that every step of a person is decreed, because parts of his soul are scattered and must be gathered. He tells of a chassid of the Rebbe Reb Elimelech, lost and dying of thirst, whose blessings over water redeemed souls trapped there for centuries, and urges the boys in camp to use every minute and stay united, unlike Korach.

title.en: The melamed and the 'uncle'

summary.en: The Rav tells a story of the Rebbe Reb Elimelech: a melamed set out through mud in torn shoes to run to the Rebbe over a wrong he saw, but the Satan, disguised as his uncle, scolded him and talked him into going back. The Rebbe told it to a young man who was about to stop coming to his minyan, saying the same uncle was at work.

title.en: Recognizing the uncle; azus dikedushah

summary.en: The Rav says the same uncle comes in many forms whenever a Jew undertakes something good, and one must recognize him: robbers only ambush the truck that carries money. He stresses peace among the boys, then the first siman of Shulchan Aruch, not to be ashamed before scoffers, and a holy boldness, as when one learns while others play ball.

title.en: Toil in tefillah and davening aloud

summary.en: The Rav teaches that tefillah, the service of the heart, needs toil like Torah, and must be lively and warm. He discusses davening in a raised voice: views differ by each soul's root, but our coarse bodies need the fire of hislahavus to break through, and praise is said aloud as the angels say it.

title.en: The first thought; use every minute

summary.en: The Rav explains that when a person wakes and thinks to get up and learn, that first message comes from the soul, while the second, which argues him back, is a reaction of imagination. He closes by urging the boys to use every opportunity in camp, a Gemara, a kapitel Tehillim, a good word to a friend, and with a brachah.

catalogTitle: שופטים ושוטרים - עשה לך רב כדי שתהיה בטל להקב"ה (שייכות לימים נוראים)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the king, the kohen and the tzaddik exist so that a Jew can become batel to Hashem through someone greater than himself, and that this bittul is the preparation for crowning Hashem on Rosh Hashanah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the kohanim's due and asks why the law that service is done standing appears in a parsha about what the people owe the kohen. He explains that Hashem ordered the world as giver and receiver: the lesser bows to the greater, and a Jew needs a rebbe. Malchus, Dovid's trait, means having nothing of one's own, like the moon and like Shabbos; Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of the world, the place of bowing. On Rosh Hashanah the King comes to us. A Jewish king exists to teach the people bittul, which is why his wealth is limited and why kings of Dovid's house, wholly batel, may sit in the Azarah as part of its building. After speaking of 'tamim tihyeh' and bitachon, he answers his question: one is batel to the kohen because the kohen stands batel before Hashem, and he closes with the great Rosh Hashanah of history.

en: Hashem ordered the world as giver and receiver: the lesser receives from the greater by bowing to him, and so a Jew needs a rebbe to receive yiras Shamayim.
Malchus, the trait of Dovid HaMelech, is having nothing of one's own, like the moon that only receives the sun's light; Shabbos and Yerushalayim share this quality.
On the Regalim Jews go up to the place of malchus, but on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur the King comes to them.
The Torah's king exists to teach the people that they and the world are nothing and only Hashem is, so that through him they choose Hashem.
Kings of Dovid's house may sit in the Azarah because they are so batel to the Mikdash that they become part of its building.
Being 'tamim' with Hashem means not searching out the future and knowing that everything is run by Hashem alone; this is bitachon.
One is batel to the kohen because the kohen stands batel before Hashem; this is why the law of standing in service is stated in the parsha of the kohanim's gifts.

title.en: The kohanim's due and standing in service

summary.en: The Rav reads the pesukim of the kohanim's due, the first of the grain, wine and oil, 'for Hashem chose him to stand and serve', from which the Gemara learns that service is done standing. He asks why this law of the avodah appears here, in a parsha about what the people owe the kohen, and not in Vayikra with the other laws of the avodah.

title.en: Malki-Tzedek, Ashrei and the need for a rebbe

summary.en: From the mitzvah of appointing a king the Rav moves to Malki-Tzedek, who blessed Avraham before blessing Hashem and so lost the kehunah, and to Ashrei, which praises the tzaddikim before Tehillah l'Dovid. He explains that Hashem ordered the world as giver and receiver, the lesser bowing to the greater, and that a Jew needs a rebbe to receive yiras Shamayim through bittul.

title.en: Dovid, Shabbos and having nothing of one's own

summary.en: The Rav explains that malchus, the trait Dovid HaMelech teaches among the seven ushpizin, means having nothing of one's own, like the moon that only reflects the sun. Shabbos is the same: on it a Jew lays aside his work and business and acknowledges that all he has comes from Hashem, and Dovid stayed equally humble after he became great.

title.en: Yerushalayim, the Shabbos of the world

summary.en: Yerushalayim, the Rav says, is the Shabbos of the world: nothing is produced there, everything is brought there, and it is the place of blessing. Jews came on the Regalim to bow to Hashem, and such true bittul needs preparation, learned by being batel to one's rebbe, who is batel to someone greater.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah: the King comes to us

summary.en: The Rav asks why there is no aliyah l'regel on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and answers that on these days, the ten days of 'seek Hashem when He is found', the King comes to us, which is why their tefillos speak of malchus. He then explains the miracle that the people stood crowded yet bowed with room: one who is batel to Hashem takes up no space.

title.en: Malki-Tzedek and the purpose of a king

summary.en: The Rav identifies Malki-Tzedek as Shem ben Noach, king of Yerushalayim and kohen, and explains that blessing Avraham first was itself his acknowledgment that Avraham was greater and could bring him to greater bittul. From here he explains 'som tasim alecha melech': a king whose role is to show the people that they and the world are nothing and to bring them to choose Hashem, unlike the king demanded in Shmuel's time 'like all the nations'.

title.en: The king's limits and the honor of the Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that the king may not have many horses, wives or silver because possessions attach to a person's soul and breed haughtiness, while the king's whole role is to teach bittul. He tells how R' Naftali Amsterdam carried a sefer so that people rising for him would rise for the sefer, and reads the king's sefer Torah that goes with him the same way: the honor is directed to Hashem.

title.en: Sitting in the Azarah; the brachah of Boneh Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav brings the halacha that no one may sit in the Azarah except kings of the house of Dovid, Rashi's source in 'to stand and serve' and the pasuk 'Dovid sat before Hashem', and the Mishneh LaMelech's doubt about the law. He adds a question on bentching: in the brachah of Boneh Yerushalayim Dovid is mentioned just before the closing, which seems to break the rule that the words before the closing must match it.

title.en: Malchus is bittul: the Girgashi, chametz, Avraham's war

summary.en: The Rav explains that malchus, the seventh like Shabbos, is bittul, and brings from the Bnei Yissaschar that even the Girgashi, a malchus of the kelipah, left Eretz Yisrael and so acknowledged Hashem's kingship. He applies this to chametz, which stands for self-importance and is nullified, and to Avraham's war with the kings, where throwing dust showed that the kings were nothing.

title.en: Kings of Dovid's house become part of the Azarah

summary.en: After the story of King Yannai, who would not stand before the Sanhedrin, the Rav explains that the kings of Dovid's house stand before the court and so can sit in judgment. They may sit in the Azarah because they are so batel to the Mikdash that they become part of its building, like its stones and wood, and this also answers why Dovid belongs right before the closing of Boneh Yerushalayim.

title.en: Elul and 'tamim tihyeh'

summary.en: The Rav says the parshiyos read in Elul are about bittul, since success on Rosh Hashanah depends on the bittul with which one crowns the King. He explains 'tamim tihyeh im Hashem Elokecha' with Rashi: to walk with Hashem wholeheartedly, not to search out the future, and to know that everything is run by Hashem alone; this is bitachon.

title.en: Bitachon in daily life

summary.en: The Rav says ordinary people too can work on bitachon, as the Chovos HaLevavos teaches, at least at certain moments. One need not envy someone with a better head or more money, since Hashem gave each person exactly what he needs; he brings Dovid strengthening himself in Hashem when everything was taken from him, and points to the constant miracles of the body: a person relies on Hashem for his heart and lungs but not for tomorrow's bread.

title.en: Becoming batel through someone greater

summary.en: One who is batel to Hashem lacks nothing and envies no one. The Rav says bittul is learned only through someone greater, criticizes students who leave the yeshiva thinking they know better than their rebbeim, and brings the Rambam on how avodah zarah began. He names three authorities, father, king and rebbe, and says the first parshiyos of Elul teach bittul to king, judge, navi and kohen.

title.en: Back to 'to stand and serve'

summary.en: Returning to his opening question, the Rav explains that one gives the kohen the first of everything because he stands in service, batel to Hashem, and one becomes batel to him; therefore the law that the avodah is done standing is stated here. A kohen who serves sitting invalidates the avodah.

title.en: The great Rosh Hashanah of history

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the great Rosh Hashanah at the end of history, when the great shofar will be blown and all will come to bow to Hashem in Yerushalayim, and says every Rosh Hashanah is a miniature of it. He closes with the wish that everyone be batel to those greater than him, come to Rosh Hashanah with bittul, and merit a good year.

catalogTitle: Kosher: Healthy Nourishment for the נשמה

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches children that what a Jew eats shapes his whole Yiddishkeit: forbidden food blocks the soul, while matzah and care with kashrus bring emunah and a special protection from Heaven.

abstract.en: The Rav tells children that Parshas Shemini, which always falls near Pesach, is linked to it: Shemini lists what may not be eaten, Pesach commands eating matzah and maror. He reads the Torah's warning against forbidden foods as hinting that they stuff up a person so that no Torah, kedushah or yiras Shamayim can enter, while matzah, which Chazal call the food of emunah, brings faith, love of Hashem. One who is careful receives protection from Heaven, as two stories show: the Yeshuos Yaakov and a buttered pancake, and a Rebbe who would not eat from untoveled plates. After the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and care with chametz on Pesach, he turns to minhagim, telling of the Shpoler Zeide and explaining the Seder custom about children not falling asleep as a plea for the geulah.

en: The Rav links Parshas Shemini, which lists the forbidden foods, to Pesach, whose mitzvah is to eat matzah and maror, and says this closeness is no coincidence.
He says being careful with what one eats is one of the greatest foundations of Yiddishkeit, since forbidden food blocks a person from Torah, kedushah and yiras Shamayim.
Matzah, called by Chazal the food of emunah, brings a person faith in Hashem, love of Hashem and a desire to learn, daven and do mitzvos.
According to the Rav, one who is careful about kashrus receives a protection from Heaven not to stumble even in things he cannot know.
He teaches that every Jewish minhag has meaning, even when one does not know its reason, and one must not treat any of them as unimportant.

candidateTopics: matzah as the food of emunah

title.en: Shemini and Pesach: what not to eat and what to eat

summary.en: The Rav notes that Shemini is read just before or just after Pesach, depending on whether the year is a leap year, and says nothing is by chance. Shemini teaches what one may not eat, and Pesach commands eating matzah and maror.

title.en: Forbidden food blocks, matzah builds emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains the Torah's warning that forbidden foods stuff up a person and keep out Torah and kedushah, while matzah, the food of emunah, brings faith and love of Hashem. He says forbidden food strengthens the yetzer hara, that one should seek the most reliable hechsher with a Rebbe's guidance, and that the careful receive protection from Heaven.

title.en: The Yeshuos Yaakov and the pancake

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Yeshuos Yaakov, served a pancake by a host rav, kept speaking in learning until it grew cold. The rebbetzin then revealed it was made with butter in a fleishig pan, and he explained that hot butter had splashed in his face when he cut it, and he took this as a sign not to eat.

title.en: The Rebbe, the fish and the untoveled plates

summary.en: The Rav retells a story he heard from a respected Yid in Yerushalayim: a visiting Rebbe chose to eat at a poor, beardless but G-d-fearing man's house, would not touch the fish, and discovered that the plates, borrowed from a bearded neighbor, were not toveled. He then told the two of them what each would be asked in the World to Come.

title.en: Heavenly protection, and the Shpoler Zeide's Seder

summary.en: The Rav says those who are careful are protected from Heaven, bringing the donkey of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair that would not eat demai and the teaching that care with even a trace of chametz brings protection all year. He then turns to minhagim and tells how the Shpoler Zeide gently rebuked his son's melamed for leaving out a line of the Seder custom.

title.en: Children not falling asleep: a plea for the geulah

summary.en: The Rav explains the Midrash on 'I am asleep but my heart is awake': Klal Yisroel sleeps in golus while Hashem keeps it awake. The Seder custom about the children not falling asleep is a plea to Hashem to redeem His children before they sink further. He closes urging care with every mitzvah, din and minhag, and blesses the children.

catalogTitle: נקודה עיקרית בפרשה זו - ביטול למנהיגים ולהקב"ה

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows that Parshas Shoftim, read at the start of Elul, is entirely about accepting authority and bittul (self-nullification) to the leaders and through them to Hashem, which is the preparation for Rosh Hashanah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by noting that Shoftim is always read at the start of Elul, so every part of it prepares for the Yamim Noraim, and that all its parshiyos (judges, king, kohen, navi) speak of accepting authority. He asks why the kohen's duty to stand during the avodah is taught here and not in Vayikra, and why Malki Tzedek lost the kehunah for blessing Avraham before Hashem. He explains that all blessing flows from giver to receiver, that malchus means having nothing of one's own, as with David, the moon, Shabbos and Yerushalayim, and that every Jew needs a rebbe through whom he learns bittul to Hashem. He explains the Davidic king's sitting in the Azarah through David's total bittul, answers his opening questions, and ends with Rosh Hashanah, when Hashem's kingship comes to every Jew, and with the great future Rosh Hashanah.

en: Every part of Parshas Shoftim (judges, king, kohen, navi) speaks of one theme: accepting authority and making oneself subordinate to those Hashem has appointed.
All blessing flows in an order of giver and receiver, from the higher to the lower, and one receives only by placing oneself, through bittul, under the one above.
Malchus (kingship) is the quality of the receiver who has nothing of his own, like the moon, Shabbos and Yerushalayim; a Jewish king is king only to the degree of his bittul to Hashem.
Every Jew needs a rebbe; through bittul to the rebbe he learns to be batel to Hashem, and only the highest king may begin directly with Hashem.
On Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur Hashem's kingship comes to every Jew wherever he is, and a person's share in Rosh Hashanah depends on his bittul and acceptance of authority, prepared for in Elul.

candidateTopics: Elul and preparation for Rosh Hashanah
Davidic kings sitting in the Azarah
Yerushalayim as center of the world

title.en: Shoftim: a parsha of accepting authority

summary.en: After a few words on the merit of being in Eretz Yisroel together with Jews, the Rav notes that Shoftim is always the first parsha of Elul and prepares for the Yamim Noraim. He shows that every part of it, judges, king, kohen and navi, is about accepting authority.

title.en: Why the kohen's standing is taught here

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that 'la'amod l'shares' teaches that the avodah must be done standing, and asks why a law of the avodah appears among the kohanim's rights in Shoftim rather than in Vayikra. He then turns to the mitzvah of appointing a king.

title.en: Malki Tzedek and the order of giver and receiver

summary.en: The Rav raises the difficulty that Malki Tzedek lost the kehunah for blessing Avraham before Hashem, while David opened Tehillim with praise of the tzaddik. He then explains that the world is built on giver and receiver, that all blessing passes through the tzaddik, and that bittul places a person like a vessel under the tap.

title.en: Receiving one's rebbe on the regel; place, time and soul

summary.en: The Rav asks why one must greet one's rebbe specifically on the festival. He explains that every soul's place in the chain of giving is set from Above, that Hashem created everything in place, time and soul, and that Yerushalayim, Shabbos and certain souls are the aspect of malchus, the receiver.

title.en: Malchus is bittul: David, the moon and Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav explains that only Hashem is truly King, and a Jewish king is king only through his bittul, like a wire plugged into the current. David is like the moon with no light of its own, hence Rosh Chodesh and the king's feast; Shabbos and shmitah teach that a person has nothing and Hashem gives everything.

title.en: David's name and Yerushalayim, which has nothing of its own

summary.en: The Rav brings the Sfas Emes that David's name begins and ends with a dalet, poverty, which stays even after all the giving. Yerushalayim, the seventh, is likewise supported by the world, yet it is blindness to think the week gives to Shabbos or the am ha'aretz to the talmid chacham; the giving flows like that to a king, and in Yerushalayim one bows in bittul.

title.en: Every Jew needs a rebbe; Hashem comes to us on Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Rav says every Jew must have a rebbe, a link to someone higher, and that this answers why one greets one's rebbe on the regel: in Yerushalayim not everyone can receive directly from Hashem. He asks why there is no aliyah l'regel on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and answers that then the King comes to every Jew; in Elul He is like a king in the field.

title.en: Bowing with room in the Mikdash; Malki Tzedek answered

summary.en: The Rav explains the miracle that the people stood crowded yet bowed with room: in the place of malchus each became nothing and took up no space. He then answers the question about Malki Tzedek: his loss revealed that everyone must first accept a rebbe, while the king of Yerushalayim, the highest, must begin with Hashem Himself; David began Tehillim with 'Ashrei ha'ish' for the people.

title.en: A king whom Hashem would choose

summary.en: On 'som tasim alecha melech asher yivchar Hashem', the Rav explains that one must choose the king Hashem would choose, not for political or party reasons. The choosing is mutual: through such a king a Jew chooses Hashem, and the purpose is fear of the king leading to fear of Hashem.

title.en: Not 'like all the nations': the king's bittul

summary.en: The Rav brings the Steipler that proud people who despair of recognition attach themselves to a party, and says a king 'like all the nations' is not the mitzvah. The essence of the king is bittul, hence the limits on his wealth and the sefer Torah he carries, as the Yesod Yosef advises a rav to take a sefer along; Shlomo at the Temple gates proclaimed that Hashem is the King of glory.

title.en: Sitting in the Azarah; the Bach's question

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Yoma that only kings of the house of David may sit in the Azarah, and Rashi, who derives it from 'la'amod l'shares' and quotes the whole verse of David sitting before Hashem. He asks why that law applies beyond the avodah and why Rashi needs the whole verse, and adds the Bach's question on the Nusach Ashkenaz ending of the blessing Boneh Yerushalayim.

title.en: The Girgashi, earth, and Avraham's dust

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the Girgashi, who left rather than fight, is the seventh nation, the aspect of malchus, which is batel to Hashem. Earth too is malchus: it never becomes tamei or forbidden because it is batel. With this he explains Avraham throwing dust at the four kings: in his bittul he showed they were nothing.

title.en: David, part of the building of Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara about Yanai that a king is neither judged nor judges, but kings of the house of David are judged, and reads 'omdos hayu ragleinu' as David speaking of himself. David's bittul made him like the dust of the Azarah, part of the Mikdash itself, so the law of standing in awe does not apply to him; this answers Rashi's long verse and the Bach's question.

title.en: The main point: bittul step by step

summary.en: The Rav states the heart of the parsha: bittul to the greater one, to one's friend, to the rebbe and so to Hashem, and that the success of Rosh Hashanah depends on it, prepared by this parsha thirty days before. He brings the Chasam Sofer on Avraham, David and Moshe, and answers the opening question: the kohen's standing is a law of mora Mikdash and bittul, so it is taught in Shoftim, like Rabbeinu Tam's view on the mezuzah.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah: Yerushalayim comes to the whole world

summary.en: The Rav explains that in Elul and on Rosh Hashanah the Mikdash comes to us, so a Jew in New York or Miami bows to Hashem on the holy mountain in Yerushalayim. Eretz Yisroel is Rosh Hashanah in place, Rosh Hashanah is Eretz Yisroel in time, and the tzaddikim are it in soul; hence the custom of traveling to the rebbe for Rosh Hashanah and the Sanhedrin sitting in the Lishkas Hagazis.

title.en: The center of the world and the great Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Rav explains why one goes up to Yerushalayim for a ruling: Rashi says the Mikdash is the highest place, and the Chasam Sofer explains that the center, where creation began, is the highest; 'al pi haTorah asher yorucha' stands at the middle of Sefer Devarim. He ends with the great future Rosh Hashanah and calls on everyone to learn the sedra, bittul and acceptance of authority.

catalogTitle: “לשכנו תדרשו ובאת שמה” - ארץ ישראל גבוה מכל הארצות. דרוש בענין דוד ואביגיל

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows that Dovid HaMelech is bound to Yerushalayim, the place 'asher yivchar Hashem', and explains through the story of Avigail and Naval that Avigail was the guardian of the eternity of Dovid's kingship, leading to Sefer Devarim and Elul as the building of Yerushalayim.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rashi that the Beis HaMikdash is higher than all places and with 'l'shichno sidreshu': the Torah does not say where the chosen place is, and Dovid, together with Shmuel, found it. Since the king too is 'asher yivchar Hashem', the chosen soul and the chosen place belong together, and Dovid is Yerushalayim. From the Midrash on Yaakov's message to Esav, which counts Avigail among his powers, he turns to the story of Dovid, Naval and Avigail. He asks why Avigail is counted among the seven prophetesses, why Hashem revealed only through Shlomo that Dovid had not sinned, and why Dovid did not think of her simple arguments. He answers with three introductions: Moshiach's soul comes hidden from the Satan, Dovid is the eternal Yerushalayim, and malchus beis Dovid is the kingship of the Shechinah. Avigail was the guardian of that eternity. He then explains Sefer Devarim as the book of teshuvah and of Yerushalayim, Elul as the time of Yerushalayim, and closes on the greatness of living in Eretz Yisrael.

en: The Torah does not reveal the chosen place or the chosen king; both must be sought, and Dovid, the chosen soul, found the chosen place.
Dovid is Yerushalayim, which is why the blessing that mentions malchus beis Dovid can end with 'boneh Yerushalayim'.
Malchus beis Dovid is not only a political kingship but a kingship of the Shechinah, so one who rebels against it is like one who denies Hashem.
Avigail was sent by Hashem as the guardian of the eternity of Dovid's kingship, keeping him from bloodshed so that Moshiach would remain unblemished.
Sefer Devarim is the book of teshuvah and of Yerushalayim, read from Shabbos Chazon until Shemini Atzeres, and the avodah of Elul is to learn it with warmth.
A Jew in Eretz Yisrael, and above all in Yerushalayim, can reach far higher with his Torah and tefillah, so every moment there is precious.

Sefer Devarim as the book of teshuvah
Elul as the time of Yerushalayim

title.en: Seeking the chosen place and the chosen king

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that the Beis HaMikdash is higher than all places and the Gemara in Zevachim that Dovid and Shmuel sat in Nayos b'Ramah searching for the site of the Mikdash, which provoked Doeg's jealousy. He notes that the Torah says only 'l'shichno sidreshu', and that the parsha of the king likewise says 'asher yivchar Hashem': both the place and the king must be found.

title.en: Dovid is Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav explains that Dovid and Yerushalayim are one, answering why the blessing mentioning malchus beis Dovid can conclude 'boneh Yerushalayim'. Each soul has its portion in Torah, and Dovid's was to find the chosen place; Doeg saw in this that Dovid was the chosen king, and the Rav adds gematrios linking 'l'shichno sidreshu' and 'b'Nayos b'Ramah' to the king 'asher yivchar'.

title.en: Yaakov's warning to Esav and the story of Naval

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash on 'vayehi li shor vachamor' in Vayishlach, where Yaakov warns Esav by listing the powers within him: Yosef, Yissachar's Torah, Moshe, Dovid and 'shifchah', which is Avigail. He asks what is frightening about Avigail and retells the story of Dovid, Naval and Avigail, who held Dovid back from killing Naval as a rebel against the kingship.

title.en: Lavan returns as Naval

summary.en: The Rav brings from the Degel, in the name of the Arizal, that Lavan was reincarnated in Naval, so Dovid was Yaakov again facing Lavan. He explains, with the Me'or Einayim, why Yaakov did not destroy Lavan: holy sparks and letters of Torah still remained in him, so Yaakov had to wait. That restraint is Avigail's power, which Yaakov invoked to warn Esav.

title.en: Avigail among the seven prophetesses

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Megillah that Avigail was one of the seven prophetesses, proven from her words 'v'lo sihyeh zos lecha l'fukah' that foretold the episode of Bas Sheva. He raises difficulties: her two arguments (Shaul is still king; Dovid's kingship is not yet known) seem so simple that Dovid should have thought of them, and a prophecy needed neither for later generations nor for Dovid himself hardly fits the count of prophecies.

title.en: Why Dovid's innocence was revealed only through Shlomo

summary.en: The Rav asks why the pesukim keep calling her 'Avigail eishes Naval'. He brings that Dovid did not sin with Bas Sheva, that Dovid still begged forgiveness, and the Gemara in Shabbos that the gates would not open for the aron until Shlomo said 'zochrah l'chasdei Dovid avdecha', when Dovid's enemies were shamed. He asks why Hashem waited until Shlomo and the Beis HaMikdash to show this.

title.en: First introduction: Moshiach's soul hidden from the Satan

summary.en: The Rav explains that Adam, Dovid and Moshiach are one soul, and that this soul must come into the world hidden from the Satan, who would otherwise oppose it. Hence 'matzasi Dovid avdi', found in Sedom through Lot's daughters, and the further stations of Moshiach's lineage; he brings Tosafos on confusing the Satan, a Midrash on the Satan demanding his share, the Yismach Moshe on the Satan's three errors, and concludes that the rumors about Dovid and Bas Sheva were allowed so the Satan would not notice.

title.en: Dovid's eternity and the kingship of the Shechinah

summary.en: In the second introduction the Rav explains that Dovid, like Yerushalayim, is eternal and bound to the Shechinah. In the third he contrasts an ordinary king, honored for the order of the state, with malchus beis Dovid, anointed with Moshe's shemen hamishchah, so that disputing it is like denying Hashem, as the Rambam writes in the twelfth principle. This secret had to stay hidden until the Beis HaMikdash was finished, with a story of a tzaddik who at his passing told the Satan he had never been his.

title.en: Dovid's knowledge and the error of ruach hakodesh

summary.en: The Rav brings that Bas Sheva was destined for Dovid from the six days of creation and, from the Zera Kodesh, that she first had to be with Uriah, as Eretz Yisrael was first with the Canaanim. Dovid knew all this by ruach hakodesh, but ruach hakodesh can err, unlike nevuah: Yaakov thought Shimshon was Moshiach. So too Dovid, seeing Avigail, felt she was his zivug and would bear the son who saves him from shame, and erred, as the Gemara in Berachos about Kilav shows.

title.en: Avigail's prophecy saves Dovid

summary.en: The Rav resolves the questions: Dovid judged Naval a rebel because of the heavenly kingship of beis Dovid he already held, and his mistaken ruach hakodesh removed his doubt. Avigail answered both kinds of kingship and told him in prophecy that she was not the mother of Shlomo; that would be Bas Sheva. Dovid obeyed a prophetess at once, and she saved the purity of Moshiach, whose kingship must be unblemished.

title.en: 'Avigail eishes Naval': guardian of Dovid's eternity

summary.en: The Rav explains that the pesukim call her 'eishes Naval' because her essential role came before she married Dovid, and that 'Avigail eishes Naval' equals in gematria 'Dovid melech Yisrael chai v'kayam'. She is the guarantee of Dovid's eternity, the protector of the point of Dovid, like 'Magen Dovid' beside 'Magen Avraham'; this is why Yaakov counted her among his powers against Esav.

title.en: Why Sefer Devarim opens with Israel's faults

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Pesach Sheni is not at the start of Bamidbar because of Israel's disgrace, and asks why Devarim does open with their sins. He answers from the Gemara that Devarim is Moshe's words: a leader's rebuke is the beauty of Klal Yisrael. He then brings Rabbeinu Bachya that the four books match the four letters of Hashem's name and the four species, and Devarim, the last hei and the esrog, stands apart, which is why it starts 'Eileh' without a vav.

title.en: Devarim, Dovid and Yerushalayim as teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav links the last hei to Dovid and Yerushalayim, 'yirah shleimah', and brings the Tanya on Tikkun Chatzos: one lacking in yiras Shamayim mourns his own portion in Yerushalayim, since every Jew has a spark of Dovid. Dovid established teshuvah, so Sefer Devarim is the book of teshuvah and of Yerushalayim, which is why it repeats 'the place Hashem will choose'.

title.en: From Shabbos Chazon to Shemini Atzeres: cleaning the esrog

summary.en: The Rav brings, via Rav Hillel Paritcher, the Berditchever's teaching that on Shabbos Chazon every Jew is shown the third Beis HaMikdash. Devarim is read from Shabbos Chazon until Shemini Atzeres, a journey to built Yerushalayim, where teshuvah from love turns sins into merits; the beginning of Devarim is the esrog's tip, and the avodah of Elul is to clean the esrog by learning Devarim with Rashi and meforshim.

title.en: The elevation of a Jew in Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: Addressing the audience in Yerushalayim, the Rav says he will not come from Brooklyn to inspect them. He shows how Devarim moves from praising Eretz Yisrael to Yerushalayim, brings Sefer Yetzirah that place, soul and time correspond, so Elul is the time of Yerushalayim, and explains 'b'chol mishlach yedchem' with the Targum: in Eretz Yisrael a Jew's reach is higher. He brings the Chasam Sofer, a Slonim saying about Napoleon not wanting to sleep, and Rashi on 'ki tov yom bachatzeirecha'.

title.en: Feeling each day as new; Elul as Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that the land should feel every day as if given today, and says a Jew in Eretz Yisrael must renew this feeling constantly. He describes Elul as entering Yerushalayim, Rosh Hashanah as the Beis HaMikdash and Yom Kippur as the Kodesh, and says every good deed there is a stone in the third Beis HaMikdash. The final minutes are badly garbled.

catalogTitle: “ראשית עריסותיכם תתנו לכהן” - שהוא ראשית שבנפש

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why a gift to a talmid chacham is likened specifically to bikkurim: both are 'reishis', and the bikkurim brought to the kohen in Yerushalayim were meant to keep every Jew bound to the talmidei chachamim who teach him the shiurim of the Torah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara that one who brings a gift to a talmid chacham is as if he brought bikkurim, and asks why bikkurim of all the priestly gifts. Through the Chasam Sofer's reading of Rashi's first comment on the Torah, he shows that the Jews, though created later, are first in Hashem's thought and are called 'reishis', as is the talmid chacham and as are bikkurim. He then raises further questions on the parsha: why bikkurim must come from the seven species, why the kohen 'of those days', why the bikkurim declaration recalls the Exodus. His answer: the seven species carry the Torah's measures, which Hashem left uncertain so Jews would always need a talmid chacham, and since the fruits change with Israel's merit, the kohen who sees bikkurim from the whole land each year can rule on them. He closes with the forty days of Elul as Eretz Yisrael in time, Ki Seitzei's message that no Jew is lost, and the hidden blessings in Ki Savo's curses.

en: A gift to a talmid chacham is like bikkurim because both are called 'reishis', the first and most important, just as the Jews are first in Hashem's thought.
The Torah's shiurim tied to the seven species were left uncertain on purpose, so that Jews would always need to ask a talmid chacham.

Since the fruits of Eretz Yisrael grow larger or smaller with Israel's merit, the kohen in Yerushalayim, who receives bikkurim of the seven species from the whole land every year, is the one able to rule on the shiurim.
Without a rebbi and a circle of G-d-fearing friends a person can fall, as even Shlomo HaMelech did once his rebbi was gone.
A person can stand in Eretz Yisrael and not be in it, as a gentile can be in the day of Shabbos without any share in Shabbos; connection comes through attachment to the talmid chacham.
Parshas Ki Savo, read in Elul, teaches that the curses hide blessings and that no Jew is truly bad; the work of Elul is to uncover the good.

title.en: Why a gift to a talmid chacham is like bikkurim

summary.en: The Rav opens with the derashah that bikkurim is the mitzvah for which Israel enters the land, and the Gemara that bringing a gift to a talmid chacham is like bringing bikkurim, and asks why bikkurim of all gifts. He then brings the Chasam Sofer on Rashi's first comment, with the mashal of the leaves of the vine and the palm who complain that the younger fruit is served while they only form the baskets.

title.en: First in thought: Israel, the Torah and reishis

summary.en: The Rav applies the mashal to the nations who claim to be older than Israel, and explains through the dispute of Tishrei and Nissan that the Torah opens with Bereishis, creation in thought, to show that Israel is first in thought. Talmidei chachamim and bikkurim are both reishis, and he explains why bikkurim go to the kohen in Yerushalayim, the place of reishis; this is the Chasam Sofer's answer.

title.en: More questions on the bikkurim parsha

summary.en: The Rav asks why the comparison is to bikkurim and not to terumah or other things called reishis; why Rashi's heavenly voice blesses the one who brought bikkurim when viduy maaser covers all gifts; what 'the kohen who will be in those days' means for bikkurim, as the Ramban asks; why the declaration tells of the Exodus; and why bikkurim come only from the seven species. He announces several introductions to answer them.

title.en: The seven species and the Torah's shiurim

summary.en: As a first introduction the Rav brings the Gemara that the seven species of the pasuk serve as the measures of the Torah: wheat, barley, grape, fig, pomegranate, olive and date. He asks why Hashem gave measures that leave us uncertain, illustrated by a builder who cannot work with an undefined measure and by the wide gap between accepted shiurim of a revi'is, and points to the Gemara that the talmidei chachamim of Eretz Yisrael are hard as iron.

title.en: One must cling to a talmid chacham

summary.en: The Rav lays down that a Jew must be attached to a talmid chacham and to a good circle of friends. He brings Shlomo HaMelech, wisest of men, who married Pharaoh's daughter only after his rebbi Shimi ben Gera died, and fell; whoever walks with the wise grows wise, and the mitzvah of 'u'vo sidbak', clinging to talmidei chachamim, is the aim of all the Torah's counsels.

title.en: Why the shiurim are uncertain

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem wanted Jews always to need the talmid chacham, so He built the whole Torah on shiurim and gave them in a way that leaves us not knowing: shofar, sukkah, tzitzis, a shochet's questions, a young couple in a new apartment all send a person to ask. This, in his view, is the reason for the uncertain measures, and the iron-hard talmidei chachamim of Eretz Yisrael are there to be used.

title.en: In Eretz Yisrael and yet not in it

summary.en: As a second introduction the Rav brings the Tzemach Hashem Litzvi, who wonders how the nations could build their house of worship on Har HaBayis, and answers that Hashem spreads the soil of the nations beneath them, so they are not truly in Eretz Yisrael. The Rav compares it to Shabbos: a gentile is in the day of Shabbos but separated from it, while a Jew's share in it depends on keeping it.

title.en: The kohen's two roles: avodah and teaching

summary.en: The Rav explains that the kohen has two tasks given to the tribe of Levi: to teach Torah to Israel and to perform the avodah in the Beis HaMikdash, and Malachi says one seeks Torah from the mouth of the kohen. He notes how many authors of the poskim and how many morei hora'ah in a beis medrash are kohanim or levi'im, as a fulfilment of that blessing.

title.en: The kohen who rules on the yearly shiurim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer's question how the shiurim can be known when the fruits of Eretz Yisrael change, as in the days of the spies, and his answer that they grow with Israel's merit, so they must be checked every year. The kohen in Yerushalayim, receiving the seven species from every part of the land, can rule on them; this is the purpose of bikkurim, which is why they come every year and only from the seven species.

title.en: Bikkurim as the bond with the talmid chacham

summary.en: The Rav returns to the questions: the 'kohen of those days' matters because the bikkurim are brought so that he can rule, and one also gains yiras Shamayim seeing the avodah. Bringing bikkurim creates a bond with the talmid chacham, and that bond is what makes a person truly in Eretz Yisrael; therefore the declaration tells of leaving Egypt, showing that the bringer has no share in the land of the nations.

title.en: Elul as Eretz Yisrael in time

summary.en: The Rav explains that Eretz Yisrael is the reishis of the world as Rosh Hashanah is the reishis of the year, citing 'from the beginning of the year to the end of the year'; the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are Eretz Yisrael in time, when Ki Savo is read. To enter them without a barrier one must go to the kohen, the rebbi or mentor, and ask how to do teshuvah and improve, and learn the parsha.

title.en: Ki Seitzei: tikkun and the ben sorer umoreh

summary.en: Returning briefly to last week's parsha, the Rav says all of Ki Seitzei is about tikkun and redemption, from the yefas to'ar with the Ohr HaChaim onward. He dwells on the ben sorer umoreh: the Gemara says it never was and never will be, which he reads as teaching that no Jew is beyond hope, and he explains Rabbi Yonasan's sitting on such a one's grave; he adds the Baal Shem Tov on Reb Yitzchak of Drohobitch.

title.en: Hidden blessings in Ki Savo's curses

summary.en: The Rav says Ki Savo, read close to Rosh Hashanah, teaches that even what looks bad is not truly bad: unlike Bechukosai, its rebuke ends without words of comfort because it is all hidden blessing. At Har Gerizim and Har Eival only the curses are written and the blessings are learned from them, and Elul is the time that turns curse into blessing.

title.en: Uncovering the good before Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that every 'hashkafah' in the Torah is for bad except in the bikkurim parsha, where gifts to the poor turn it to blessing, and says no Jew is truly bad. The work of Elul and Rosh Hashanah is to uncover the good hidden in oneself and turn every hardship to good, learning Ki Savo with its commentaries; he closes with a blessing for a good year.

catalogTitle: טומאת יולדת and the ענין of אליהו (Connection to ניסן)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the tumah of a woman after childbirth as the emptying of holiness, and shows how the bris, through Eliyahu HaNavi, cuts that tumah short, tying the parsha to Nisan, the month of Chesed and of Eliyahu.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why a woman becomes tamei through giving birth, when for nine months she carried a 'beis medrash' in which an angel taught the child Torah. He brings the Or HaChaim's answer to why a Jewish body is tamei in a tent and a non-Jew's is not: impurity gathers where holiness has left, like flies at an emptied honey jar. So too the mother, once the holiness of the child leaves her. Since a girl's Torah is of a lesser degree, he asks why a girl brings fourteen days and a boy only seven, and answers that the bris brings Eliyahu HaNavi, and the mother, as a close relative who shares in its joy, has her tumah cut off. He ties this to Nisan: in a leap year Tazria is read first in Nisan, the month of Eliyahu, of Chesed and of return, and he closes with the Chozeh of Lublin's notebook showing that the first twelve days of Nisan govern the year.

en: Tumah comes where holiness has departed: the greater the holiness that left, the greater the tumah, which is why a Jewish body is tamei in a tent and a non-Jew's is not.
A woman becomes tamei after birth because the holiness of the child, who learned Torah with an angel inside her, has emptied out of her.
After a boy the tumah lasts only seven days because the bris brings Eliyahu HaNavi, and the mother, as a close relative sharing its joy, has her tumah cut off.
In a leap year Tazria, with its bris and Eliyahu, is the first parsha read in Nisan, the month in which the Jewish people are preoccupied with Eliyahu and the Geulah.
Nisan is the month of Chesed and Tishrei the month of Din, as seen in the right and left sides and in the letters of Aviv and Tishrei.
The first twelve days of Nisan govern the whole year, even more than the Ten Days of Teshuvah, but they are days of Chesed, not of fasting and Selichos.

the first twelve days of Nisan

title.en: Why is a woman tamei after birth?

summary.en: The Rav opens with the parsha of a woman who gives birth and notes the Or HaChaim's teaching that one may not remove tzaraas by hand. He then asks why a mother, who carried a 'beis medrash' where an angel taught the child and who brings Mashiach closer with each child, should become tamei.

title.en: Flies at the honey jar: tumah where holiness left

summary.en: The Rav brings the Or HaChaim's question why a dead Jew is tamei in a tent and a non-Jew is not, and his parable of flies swarming an emptied honey jar more than a garbage can. He applies it to the mother: the holiness of the child has emptied out of her, so she becomes tamei.

title.en: Why fourteen days for a girl? Kinship

summary.en: The Rav asks why a girl brings two weeks of tumah when her Torah is of a lesser degree than a boy's, and begins his answer with the laws of family kinship: the seven relatives for whom a kohen becomes tamei, and the father's mitzvah of milah, by which the father, mohel and sandak may wear Shabbos clothing on Tisha B'Av.

title.en: Eliyahu at the bris cuts off the tumah

summary.en: The Rav asks why the mother may also eat on a postponed Tisha B'Av when she has no part in the mitzvah, and answers that Eliyahu HaNavi comes to every bris, bringing a taste of the future and atonement; as a relative she shares that joy. Therefore after a boy the bris interrupts her tumah at seven days, while after a girl it runs fourteen.

title.en: Tazria opens Nisan: the month of Eliyahu

summary.en: The Rav explains that each sedra reflects its time: in a leap year Tazria is the first sedra read in Nisan, followed by Shabbos HaGadol, whose haftarah ends with Eliyahu. He describes how Nisan and the Seder are filled with longing for Eliyahu, with tzaddikim waiting by the door on Erev Pesach.

title.en: The law of return: Yovel

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rashab's remark that scientists state laws of nature without knowing why, as with a knife cutting challah, while Torah knows the reasons. He explains the natural law that everything returns to its source, which in loshon hakodesh is called yovel, and ties it to teshuvah, the shofar and the fiftieth level that comes on Pesach night.

title.en: Right is Chesed, left is Din

summary.en: The Rav explains that the right side is Chesed and the left Din, and that a Jew's avodah is to give priority to Chesed and bind Din. He shows this in dressing right first and tying the left shoe first, in the Akeidah, in writing from right to left, in Esav and Yishmael as the impurities of Yitzchak and Avraham, and in the longer right strap of the tefillin.

title.en: Nisan of Chesed, Tishrei of Din

summary.en: The Rav describes two sets of seasons: spring, starting with Nisan, when nature blooms with Chesed, and winter, starting with Tishrei, a time of Din and contraction, like water freezing into ice. He reads Aviv as aleph-beis from the right and Tishrei as the letters backwards, and asks why the month is called Aviv and not with a gimel.

title.en: The Chozeh of Lublin's notebook

summary.en: The Rav tells the story the Bnei Yissaschar records of the Chozeh of Lublin, who on each of the first twelve days of Nisan wrote what would happen in one month of the year, and left the fifth month blank, the month in which he passed away. From this he concludes that these twelve days govern the whole year.

title.en: Nisan: revival and teshuvah with love

summary.en: The Rav notes that Rosh Chodesh Nisan is the day the Mishkan was erected, that the Geulah is hoped for in Nisan, and that the haftarah of the dry bones on Shabbos Chol HaMoed shows Pesach as a time of revival. He says every Jew should come alive through teshuvah on Pesach, a teshuvah of love expressed in Shir HaShirim, and closes with wishes for the Geulah.

catalogTitle: ביכורים - פועל דמיוני שבני ישראל' שהם שבעת המינים של הקב"ה' ישובו לארץ ישראל

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains bikkurim as a symbolic prophetic act for the return of the Jewish people, the 'seven species' of Hashem, to Eretz Yisrael, and builds from it the idea that Rosh Hashana is the Beis Hamikdash in time, to which every Jew brings himself as bikkurim with freshness.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Nechemia's words on Rosh Hashana and the Chasam Sofer's parable of the prisoner who rejoices in the king's coronation: joy in Hashem's kingship is a Jew's merit in judgment. He then asks why the Torah says bikkurim are the merit for entering the land, though they were brought only after settling it, and why Arami oved avi is said with them. Through the Ohr HaChaim on the fifty gates and the count of fifty mentions of the Exodus, he shows that Arami oved avi holds the future redemption. Bikkurim, from the seven species that stand for seven kinds of Jews, are a po'el dimyoni, a symbolic act like Yirmiyahu's purchase of a field, assuring the ingathering. Rosh Hashana is the reishis of time as the Mikdash is the reishis of place, so on Rosh Hashana the Mikdash comes to every Jew. He closes with Moshe Rabbeinu's prayer, renewal of life, and serving Hashem with freshness and zerizus.

en: Rejoicing in Hashem's kingship on Rosh Hashana, more than worrying about one's own judgment, is itself a Jew's salvation in judgment.
Bikkurim from the seven species are a po'el dimyoni, a symbolic act that strengthens the promise that the seven kinds of Jews will be brought back to Yerushalayim.
Arami oved avi contains the fiftieth mention of the Exodus, which holds the power of the final redemption from the fiftieth gate.
Rosh Hashana is to time what the Mikdash is to place, the point of reishis from which the whole year flows, so on Rosh Hashana the Mikdash comes to every Jew.
Time is greater than place: the destruction ruled only over the place of the Mikdash, not over its time.
Rosh Hashana renews the breath of life; a Jew should ask to serve Hashem with freshness and zerizus all year, as one who ripens first like bikkurim.
