title.en: Joy in the King's coronation on Rosh Hashana

summary.en: The Rav opens with Nechemia telling the weeping people on Rosh Hashana to eat and rejoice, and brings the Chasam Sofer's parable of the imprisoned minister who dances on the king's coronation day and is pardoned for it. Rejoicing in Hashem's kingship is a Jew's merit in judgment, and the crying of Rosh Hashana is sweetened by joy.

title.en: Questions on the parsha of bikkurim

summary.en: The Rav brings Chazal that bikkurim are the merit for entering the land and asks how, since bikkurim were brought only after conquest and settlement. He also asks why Arami oved avi and the Exodus are said with bikkurim, and why the bringing of bikkurim was celebrated with a procession like no other mitzvah.

title.en: Arami oved avi and the fifty gates

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Haggadah tells the Exodus through Arami oved avi and not through the fuller parshiyos of Shemos. He brings the Ohr HaChaim that the Jews in Egypt fell into forty-nine gates of impurity, and that before Mashiach, with the power of Torah, they will come out even from the fiftieth; the power of the Exodus comes from the fifty gates of binah.

title.en: The fiftieth mention of the Exodus

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Exodus is mentioned fifty times in the Torah in a way of praise, and that the fiftieth mention holds the key to the future redemption. Using the Chasam Sofer against the Magen Avraham on what counts as remembering the Exodus, he excludes other verses and arrives at Arami oved avi as the fiftieth, which is why Chazal chose it for the telling.

title.en: The seven species and the po'el dimyoni

summary.en: The Rav explains that the seven species are seven kinds of Jews, from wheat down to the pomegranate, the empty ones who are still full of mitzvos. He then introduces the po'el dimyoni, a symbolic act that strengthens a prophecy, from the Ramban on Yaakov's arrow and from Yirmiyahu buying Chanamel's field before the destruction.

title.en: Bikkurim as a sign of the ingathering

summary.en: The Rav concludes that bringing bikkurim of the seven species to the Mikdash is a po'el dimyoni that the seven kinds of Jews will be brought back to Yerushalayim after the exile. This answers why bikkurim are the merit for the land, why they were brought with song like the future return, and why Arami oved avi is said with them; it also prepares a Jew for the Rosh Hashana prayers for the redemption.

title.en: Reishis of place and reishis of time

summary.en: From the verse that Hashem's eyes are on Eretz Yisrael 'from the beginning of the year', the Rav explains that Eretz Yisrael and the Mikdash are the reishis of place, from which the world was created, and Rosh Hashana is the reishis of time, holding the whole year. Bikkurim, fruit that ripened first, carry a spark of reishis and therefore belong in the Mikdash.

title.en: A Jew brings himself as bikkurim

summary.en: The Rav says that on Rosh Hashana a Jew must bring himself as bikkurim, a new creation, to the Mikdash, because Rosh Hashana is the Mikdash in time and Yom Kippur at Ne'ilah is the Kodesh HaKodashim. But not everyone is let into Tziyon; one must prepare for it.

title.en: Elul's tears and the shofar of joy

summary.en: The Rav explains that Elul is the time to cry and regret one's sins, as the Zohar reads 'a month of days', so that on Rosh Hashana the crying is a different kind, a crying of joy, and the shofar is a song of Hashem's renewed kingship. 'Seek Hashem when He is found' refers to the ten days, when the Mikdash comes to every prepared Jew.

title.en: Why there is no aliya l'regel on Rosh Hashana

summary.en: The Rav asks why there is a mitzvah to go up to Yerushalayim on the three festivals but not on Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur, and answers that on these days the Mikdash comes to each Jew in time. This is why one prostrates on Yom Kippur even today, and he explains a custom that the chazan begins 'Hamelech' from his place before reaching the amud.

title.en: Time is greater than place

summary.en: The Rav shows that time is higher than place, from the Torah opening with 'Bereishis' and from the laws of improper intent in offerings, and concludes that the destruction ruled only over the place of the Mikdash, not over Shabbos and the festivals. On Rosh Hashana a Jew stands in the Mikdash of time and prays mainly for Hashem's kingship over the world.

title.en: Moshe's prayer and Eretz Yisrael above the heavens

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash on Moshe's word 'hen' and asks about the order of 'the heavens, the heavens of heavens, and the earth'. He explains why Moshe instituted asking Hashem to open one's lips before prayer only at the end of forty years: on reaching the land he felt the holiness of Eretz Yisrael, which the Chasam Sofer says is holier than the heaven above chutz la'aretz.

title.en: Why Moshe did not need it on Rosh Hashana

summary.en: The Rav explains the order of the verse and Moshe's plea to enter the land, then asks why Moshe did not feel the need for this prayer on the forty Rosh Hashanas in the desert, when the holiness of the Mikdash came to every Jew. He answers with the dispute between the Rambam and Ramban whether prayer is a daily mitzvah or only in a time of distress, and says Moshe was never in distress on Rosh Hashana.

title.en: Chaim as freshness, death as aging

summary.en: The Rav notes that bikkurim, unlike other gifts, must be brought to the Mikdash. He then explains that Chava ate on Rosh Hashana, the day the breath of life was given, and brought death, which he defines as aging, while chaim is freshness; on Rosh Hashana a Jew must renew himself and serve Hashem with chiddush. The Mikdash is the place of reishis where aging has no rule.

title.en: No sleep in the Mikdash; fresh years

summary.en: The Rav says that in the Mikdash there was freshness and no sleep, bringing the Levi whose clothes were burned for sleeping on watch, and the practice not to sleep on Rosh Hashana. He tells how a chassid answered the Baal HaTanya's blessing for long life that he wants fresh years, and asks for freshness in davening, Shabbos and Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: The young man who danced on Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav tells of a young man who danced for an hour every Shabbos, whose wife complained, and how an elder chassid explained that one who won a million dollars would dance too. He compares it to crowds cheering at a ball game and says one should daven and learn with such freshness every day, as if Shabbos had never come before.

title.en: Alive, not dead; souls in the first fruit

summary.en: The Rav says a Jew should ask on Rosh Hashana to serve Hashem alive and not lifeless, citing 'I shall not die but live' and the daily prayer of the Amora'im to rise early with a united heart. He explains that souls are in fruits and a blessing elevates them, and that a fruit which ripened before the rest holds a precious soul with zerizus, which is why it is brought to the Mikdash.

title.en: Why bikkurim go to the Kohen; zerizus

summary.en: The Rav explains that a Jew fears he cannot elevate such a precious fruit himself, so he gives it to the Kohen as his messenger, using the Baal Shem Tov's teaching that food is bound to the root of one's soul. He concludes that the parsha of bikkurim calls for zerizus and freshness, which awakens Hashem's zerizus to hasten the redemption, and blesses the listeners for a good Rosh Hashana.

catalogTitle: ביאור מדרש נפלא - עשה מצוה זו שבשבילה תיכנס לארץ (שייכות לפרשת כי תצא)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the Midrash that bikkurim is the mitzvah through which one enters the Land: a gift to a talmid chacham counts as bikkurim, and bonding with the talmid chacham, whom one must ask about the Torah's shiurim, is what truly brings a Jew into Eretz Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash calling bikkurim the mitzvah for whose sake Israel will enter the Land, and asks how this can be, since bikkurim applied only after the Land was conquered and settled. Following the Chasam Sofer, he explains that a gift to a talmid chacham is like bikkurim, because both are called 'reishis', the first and primary thing for whose sake the world was made. He then raises further questions: why bikkurim rather than terumah, why the bas kol blesses specifically bikkurim, why it must go to 'the kohen in those days', and why only from the seven species. After several introductions on the seven species as the source of the Torah's shiurim, on the need for a rebbe, on the hidden border around Eretz Yisrael, and on the kohen as teacher, he answers that bikkurim exists so that the kohen will learn and teach the yearly shiurim. He applies this to Elul and closes with Ki Seitzei and the tochachah of Ki Savo.

en: Bringing a gift to a talmid chacham counts as bringing bikkurim, because both the talmid chacham and bikkurim are called 'reishis'.
Before bikkurim could be brought to Yerushalayim, the mitzvah was fulfilled by bringing gifts to a talmid chacham, and through it Israel merited to enter the Land.
The seven species are the source of the Torah's shiurim, and the Torah left the shiurim unclear so that Jews would always have to go and ask a talmid chacham.
Since the fruits of Eretz Yisrael grow larger or smaller with the merits of the people, the kohen in Yerushalayim, receiving bikkurim from every region, could fix the shiurim anew each year.
One can live in Eretz Yisrael and not be in it, just as one can stand in the day of Shabbos without having a share in it; attachment to a talmid chacham is what brings a Jew truly into the Land.
Elul is the 'Eretz Yisrael of time', and to enter it one must come to the 'kohen' of today, a rebbe, a friend or a sefer, and ask how to do teshuvah and serve Hashem.
The curses of the tochachah are hidden blessings; Elul is the time to reveal the good hidden in every Jew.

title.en: The Midrash and the question

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that bikkurim is the mitzvah for whose sake Israel will enter the Land, and the question of the meforshim: bikkurim applied only after the Land was conquered and settled. He adds the Gemara that a gift to a talmid chacham is like bikkurim, and asks why bikkurim of all gifts.

title.en: The leaves and the fruits

summary.en: Following the Chasam Sofer, the Rav tells the mashal of the leaves of the vine and the palm who complain that they are older than the grapes and dates yet serve them as baskets; the owner answers that he planted the tree for the fruit. The nations make the same claim against Israel.

title.en: Reishis: the talmid chacham and bikkurim

summary.en: The Rav explains that the world was created in thought in Tishrei and in deed in Nisan, and the Torah opens with Bereishis to show that the thought comes first: Israel, the Torah and the talmid chacham are 'reishis'. Since bikkurim too is reishis, a gift to a talmid chacham is like bikkurim, and before the Land was settled this was the mitzvah through which Israel merited it.

title.en: Four questions on bikkurim

summary.en: The Rav asks why bikkurim rather than terumah, which is holier; why the bas kol after viduy maaser blesses specifically bikkurim; why bikkurim must go to 'the kohen in those days', with the Ramban's question; why the declaration and the story of leaving Mitzrayim belong to bikkurim; and why bikkurim come only from the seven species.

title.en: The seven species and the shiurim

summary.en: As a first introduction, the Rav brings the Gemara that the verse of the seven species teaches the Torah's shiurim, and lists the measures learned from each species. He asks why the Torah gave measures that remain unclear, comparing it to a builder told to use an unknown measure, and notes the disputes over shiurim today.

title.en: No Jew can stand without a rebbe

summary.en: The Rav lays down the rule that a Jew must attach himself to a talmid chacham and a good chevra. Even Shlomo HaMelech, while his rebbe Shimi ben Gera lived, did not marry Pharaoh's daughter; afterwards he stumbled. He brings that cleaving to talmidei chachamim is cleaving to Hashem, and that the whole Torah is built on shiurim.

title.en: Unclear shiurim send one to the talmid chacham

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem gave so many shiurim and left them unknown so that a Jew would have to go to the talmid chacham at every step, and that in Heaven they rule like the talmid chacham. He gives examples from daily life and reads 'a land whose stones are iron' as referring to the talmidei chachamim of Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: In Eretz Yisrael yet not in it

summary.en: As a second introduction, the Rav brings the Tzemach Hashem LiTzvi, who asks how the nations could defile the holy place, and answers that a strip of foreign land is spread under their feet, so that they are never truly in Eretz Yisrael. He compares it to Shabbos: a person who does not keep it stands in the day but has a partition between him and Shabbos.

title.en: The kohen as teacher and posek

summary.en: As a third introduction, the Rav explains that the kohen has two roles: the avodah in the Beis HaMikdash and teaching Torah, as in 'they shall teach Your laws to Yaakov'. This is why the passuk of the zaken mamrei speaks of 'the kohen who stands to serve', and why the lips of the kohen guard knowledge; he notes how many poskim and teachers in his beis medrash are kohanim and levi'im.

title.en: Bikkurim: to learn the yearly shiurim

summary.en: The Rav brings a teshuvah of the Chasam Sofer: how can shiurim be fixed by the fruits of Eretz Yisrael when they once were huge? The answer is that they grow with Israel's merits and must be measured each year. From this the Rav concludes that bikkurim of the seven species come to the kohen so that he can fix the shiurim, which answers why only the seven species and why the bas kol says 'repeat it next year'.

title.en: The kohen of your days and entering the Land

summary.en: The Rav answers the Ramban: since the purpose of bikkurim is to learn, one must go to the kohen of one's own days. Without attachment to a talmid chacham a Jew falls, as even Shlomo did; with it he becomes an ehrliche Jew and truly enters Eretz Yisrael. This is why he declares 'I have come to the Land' and tells of leaving Mitzrayim, the land of the nations.

title.en: Elul, the Eretz Yisrael of time

summary.en: The Rav explains that Eretz Yisrael is the 'reishis' of place as Rosh Hashanah is the reishis of time; with the Meshech Chochmah he says that in Eretz Yisrael it is Rosh Hashanah all year. The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are the Eretz Yisrael of the year, and one can be in them without being in them.

title.en: Coming to the kohen today

summary.en: The Rav applies the Midrash: to have a share in Rosh Hashanah one must come to the 'kohen', ask how to do teshuvah, how to daven and how to become better. The kohen today can be a rebbe, friends, or the author of a sefer, whose soul is in his words. The kohen's hand under the owner's hand shows that the guide lifts a person up, and one must learn Parshas Ki Savo.

title.en: Ki Seitzei: tikkun, geulah and the ben sorer

summary.en: The Rav briefly reviews Parshas Ki Seitzei as a parsha of tikkun and geulah, mentioning the yefas toar, tzitzis and Amalek. He dwells on the ben sorer umoreh: the Gemara says there never was one, yet one Tanna says he sat on his grave. The Rav explains that no Jew is ever beyond hope; the one that Tanna saw later became a tzaddik.

title.en: The tochachah as hidden blessing

summary.en: The Rav explains that the curses of Ki Savo are covered blessings, as the sefarim say, and that what looks bad in a Jew is not truly bad. Rashi on 'hashkifah' shows that even a harsh look turns to blessing through matnos aniyim. Elul is the time to reveal the good hidden in a Jew and to turn judgment into mercy; he closes with a brachah for a good year.

catalogTitle: An Explanation of The צרעת of גחזי and his (הפטרה( תיקון

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why Gehazi and his sons could not be cured of their tzaraas, how their good tidings to the starving city were blocked, and why even Gehazi is not lost forever.

abstract.en: The Rav learns the end of the haftarah of Naaman, where Elisha refuses payment for the cure, and then the chapters of the four metzora'im outside besieged Shomron, whom the Gemara identifies as Gehazi and his sons. He asks how the Gemara knows this and why the Navi records their whole reasoning, from which the Gemara in Avodah Zarah learns the halacha of chayei sha'ah. Bringing the Me'or Einayim that whoever brings good tidings receives the aspect of Eliyahu HaNavi, and the Maharal that all healing comes from the eighth level above nature, he explains that the lepers hoped to be healed by announcing the good news. The king's irrational refusal, shown by his acceptance of a weak two-horse search, kept the curse in force. Yet no Jew is rejected forever: every year Jews learn Gehazi's halacha, raising him toward his tikkun, and Pesach, like Yovel, brings freedom to every Jew.

en: The Gemara knows the four lepers were Gehazi and his sons because any other metzora would have gone to Elisha to be healed; only those under Elisha's eternal curse could not.
The lepers' reasoning, that a doubtful chance of life outweighs certain death, is the source in the Gemara for permitting a risky treatment despite the loss of chayei sha'ah.
Whoever brings good tidings receives within himself the aspect of Eliyahu HaNavi, and all healing comes from that level above death and illness.
King Yehoram's refusal to act on the lepers' report was irrational, so that Gehazi would not become the bearer of the good news and Elisha's curse would stand.
No Jew is rejected forever: each year that Jews learn the halacha Gehazi taught, he rises a rung toward his tikkun.
Pesach, like Yovel, is a time of freedom when everyone who was pushed away returns, and it has the power to bring every Jew to his tikkun.

title.en: The haftarah and the healing of Naaman

summary.en: The Rav notes which haftarah is read this year and why, then gives the background of Naaman, the Aramean general whose tzaraas Elisha cured by having him immerse seven times in the Yarden.

title.en: Elisha refuses payment; Naaman's requests

summary.en: The Rav explains why Elisha refused Naaman's gift, as a kiddush Hashem and for fear of idolatrous money, and why Elisha allowed Naaman, a non-Jew keeping the seven mitzvos, to bow outwardly in his king's temple while a Jew may not.

title.en: Gehazi's curse and the four lepers

summary.en: The Rav tells how Gehazi lied to Naaman, took payment, and was cursed by Elisha that Naaman's tzaraas would cling to him and his children forever. He then introduces the four lepers outside besieged Shomron, whom the Gemara identifies as Gehazi and his sons, and asks how the Gemara knows this.

title.en: The lepers' reasoning and chayei sha'ah

summary.en: The Rav reads the lepers' reasoning to surrender to Aram rather than die of hunger, asks why the Navi records it at length, and brings the Gemara in Avodah Zarah that learns from it that a sick person may undergo a risky surgery despite losing chayei sha'ah.

title.en: Aram flees; the lepers bring the news

summary.en: The Rav describes how Aram fled at the sound of chariots, which Chazal say were held back from the hail in Mitzrayim, how the lepers first hoarded gold and clothing, showing Gehazi's greed again, and then decided that keeping quiet on a day of good tidings was wrong and told the gatekeepers.

title.en: The king's suspicion and the officer's end

summary.en: The Rav reads how King Yehoram suspected a trap, how five horses were proposed but he sent only two, and asks why. The search finds Aram gone, the people plunder the camp, food becomes cheap as Elisha foretold, and the officer who mocked the prophecy is trampled to death.

title.en: Good tidings and Eliyahu HaNavi

summary.en: The Rav brings the Me'or Einayim that whoever brings good tidings receives the aspect of Eliyahu HaNavi, who is in charge of good tidings. Through the Maharal he explains that Eliyahu, who never died, belongs to the eighth level above the seven days of creation, the source of all healing.

title.en: Why Gehazi was not healed; the king's refusal

summary.en: The Rav answers how the Gemara knows the lepers were Gehazi and his sons: anyone else would have been healed by Elisha. He explains that the lepers hoped to undo the curse by bringing good tidings, but the king irrationally refused to accept their news, so the curse remained.

title.en: Two horses and 'the house of the king'

summary.en: The Rav proves the king's irrationality: he refused to act on strong logic, yet opened the gates on the word of two riders, an insufficient search. He also explains why the lepers' report went to 'the house of the king' while the searchers told the king himself.

title.en: No Jew is lost forever

summary.en: The Rav raises the principle that no one is ever cast away from Klal Yisrael, brings the Pri Tzaddik that Gehazi was healed in the merit of his teshuvah and good tidings, and tells the Gemara's story of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachya and his rejected student, which criticizes both him and Elisha for pushing away with both hands.

title.en: Gehazi, teacher of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav shows that the halacha of entering a doubtful risk for healing, which overrides chayei sha'ah and therefore Shabbos, comes from Gehazi's words, so Gehazi became the teacher of all Klal Yisrael. Measure for measure, he who kept talmidim from Elisha now has all Jews as talmidim, and each year this raises him toward his tikkun.

title.en: The trampled officer, Pesach and every Jew's tikkun

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rema MiPano that the elder trampled in the Azarah on Erev Pesach was a gilgul of the officer trampled in Shomron, and explains that had he lived until Pesach, a time of freedom like Yovel, he would have had his tikkun. He concludes that these haftaros before Pesach teach that every Jew will have his tikkun.

catalogTitle: “ומל ה' אלוקיך את לבבך ואת לבב” - מצוות מילה שעל ה' לקיים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that in Elul Hashem Himself performs the 'milah of the heart', uncovering the hidden love for Him in every Jew, so that each person can seize Elul from the yetzer hara, fly up to Hashem, and come to Rosh Hashanah with joy and a prayer to fulfill the purpose of his creation.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, which he compares to the forty days in which an embryo is formed, when prayer can still decide whether the coming year is blessing or curse. He brings the Ba'al HaTurim that 'umal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha' hints at Elul: Hashem circumcises the heart and reveals the Divine Name and the hidden love hidden beneath it. On the twenty-fifth of Elul, the day the light was created, this light shines into every Jew. Elul was seized by Yaakov from Esav, and its mazal is the maiden who escaped a fallen angel by taking his wings; so too a Jew must not despair but take the yetzer hara's own wings and fly to Hashem. He develops Shevet Dan, the lost tribe whose task is returning lost things, and Shimshon's prayer 'just this once'. He ends with the joy of Rosh Hashanah as Hashem's coronation and with Chana's prayer that nothing is created for nothing.

en: The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are like the first forty days of an embryo's formation, when prayer can still determine whether the year will be blessing or curse.
In Elul Hashem Himself performs the milah of the heart, uncovering the Divine Name and the hidden love for Him that lies in every Jewish heart.
Elul belongs to Yaakov only because he seized it from Esav, so a Jew must not make peace with the yetzer hara's hold on him but seize himself back.
A Jew who feels conquered should take the yetzer hara's own fire and wings, fly up to the Throne of Glory and ask Hashem for help, even only once.
Shevet Dan represents lost souls, and their task, and the task of Elul, is returning what was lost; Hashem Himself does this, gathering the dispersed even from the ends of the heavens.
The avodah of Rosh Hashanah is one of joy at Hashem's coronation, and its teshuvah is to fit oneself into His kingdom rather than dwell on personal troubles.
On Rosh Hashanah one asks, like Chana, that one's existence not be in vain but fulfill the purpose for which one was created.

candidateTopics: the twenty-fifth of Elul and the creation of light
Shevet Dan and returning lost things

title.en: Elul's forty days as the forming of the year

summary.en: The Rav notes that Elul opens with 'blessing and curse' and the Shabbos before Rosh Hashanah repeats it, and compares the forty days to Yom Kippur to the forty days of an embryo's formation, when prayer still decides if the child is male or female, which the Ba'al HaTurim links to blessing and curse.

title.en: Hashem circumcises the heart in Elul

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al HaTurim that 'umal Hashem Elokecha es levavcha' hints at Elul, and explains that beneath the orlah of the heart lies the Divine Name and a hidden love; 'mi ya'aleh lanu hashamayma' shows that one ascends to heaven through milah, and the revealed love becomes the Jew's very life.

title.en: The twenty-fifth of Elul and 'Yehi Or'

summary.en: The Rav explains that today, the day the world's creation began and light was created, the light shines again into every Jew and reveals his hidden love; he ties the twenty-sixth day of Elul and the twenty-sixth verse of the sedra to the Divine Name, and the separation of light from darkness to every Jew becoming a tzaddik with a Gan Eden in his heart.

title.en: Elul seized from Esav; the maiden and the wings

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar's Midrash that Yaakov seized Elul from Esav, and a Midrash about a maiden who took a fallen angel's wings, flew to the Throne of Glory and became the mazal of Elul; from this he teaches that one must take the yetzer hara's wings and fly to Hashem.

title.en: No Jewish soul is sold forever

summary.en: The Rav explains that the yetzer hara concentrates on the loftiest souls, and that a Jew must never say he is sold to it; from the redemption of a Jew sold to a gentile he shows that every soul must be redeemed, through a friend's encouragement, a tzaddik, or Hashem Himself.

title.en: Shevet Dan, the lost souls

summary.en: The Rav brings that Shevet Dan were the stragglers expelled from the Clouds of Glory whom Amalek attacked at Refidim, and that as the rear guard they returned lost objects; their nature as lost souls gives them the task of returning what was lost, tied to the great shofar that gathers the lost.

title.en: Elul as the time of Dan's camp

summary.en: The Rav lays out the four camps parallel to the Chumashim, from Yehudah and Bereishis to Dan and Devarim, and explains that Elul is Dan's time of returning lost things; Hashem Himself returns the dispersed in this week's sedra, and the whole season to Shemini Atzeres is one long shofar blast bringing them back under the wings of the Shechinah.

title.en: Shimshon's prayer: just this once

summary.en: The Rav advises taking the yetzer hara's energy and flying with it to the Throne of Glory, since even a lost Jew keeps a thread of heaven; he brings that Shimshon was from Dan and prayed 'remember me, strengthen me just this once', teaches that breaking the yetzer hara once is enough, and tells of a tzaddik who drove out a dybbuk because he had done teshuvah.

title.en: Elul as a city of refuge

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that Elul is a city of refuge, hinted in 'ina leyado vesamti lecha makom', and urges not to wait while the door is open; he explains 'lecha amar libi' with Rashi, that Hashem sends His message through a Jew's heart.

title.en: Nasan the prophet and 'velo anachnu'

summary.en: The Rav explains that every chapter of Tehillim belongs to every Jew, so Nasan the prophet comes to each one; he then reads 'velo anachnu' both as 'not' and as 'His', and explains that despite what happened to the six million and the heretical talk it brought, Hashem's silence is strength and a Jew must know he belongs to Hashem.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah as Hashem's joy and coronation

summary.en: The Rav explains that the avodah of Tishrei differs from Elul: Hashem is a ba'al simchah as at a bris, so even the weeping must come from joy; he brings Nechemiah's 'do not weep' and a parable of a prisoner who danced on the day of his trial because it was the king's jubilee, and concludes that the teshuvah of Rosh Hashanah is fitting into Hashem's kingdom.

title.en: Chana's prayer: nothing is created in vain

summary.en: The Rav asks why the remembering of barren women belongs to Rosh Hashanah, brings that the laws of tefilah and the nine blessings of Rosh Hashanah come from Chana, and explains her argument that everything Hashem created has a purpose; so on Rosh Hashanah one asks to fit into the purpose of creation.

title.en: Why Chana spoke of nursing

summary.en: The Rav asks why Chana mentioned nursing rather than other organs, and answers from the Gemara that it is better to pray about hunger than plague, with a story of a tzaddik who saved a sick man through the gates of parnasah; he adds that Chana saw Eli's unworthy sons and asked for a son who would anoint two kings, and closes with praying on Rosh Hashanah to fulfill one's purpose.

catalogTitle: “מחוטב עציך עד שואב מימך” - חשיבות דורות השפלים (התעוררות לר"ה)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that 'from the hewer of your wood to the drawer of your water' in Parshas Nitzavim refers to the last, darkest generations, whose hard-won service of Hashem is as precious as that of the greatest generations, and he draws from this the strength with which a Jew comes to Rosh Hashana.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rosh Hashana as the day man was created and with the Gemara's account of David and Shmuel searching out the place of the Beis HaMikdash: the highest place in the world, lowered so that water could reach the mikveh. The king's soul, the place of the Mikdash and Rosh Hashana are each the 'head' that includes everything after it. Turning to Nitzavim, he asks what 'from the hewer of your wood to the drawer of your water' means. Following the Tanya's picture of all generations as one body, he explains that these are the last generations, whose learning and davening in the darkness of hester panim feel like chopping wood and drawing water, yet before Hashem all are equal, perhaps even more precious. A Jew must know his worth. He then speaks of Rosh Hashana as the root of the year, of the shofar as the voice of a Jew's inner self that only Hashem understands, of a new yetzer tov each year, and of davening for every need.

en: Rosh Hashana, the place of the Beis HaMikdash and the soul of the king are each a 'head' that contains all the times, places and souls that follow.
'From the hewer of your wood to the drawer of your water' refers to the last generations before Moshiach, the 'heels' of the one body that all the generations form.
In these generations learning and davening are hard labor without seeing results, like chopping wood and drawing water, yet before Hashem they stand equal to the greatest generations.
A Jew must know his worth before Hashem, because that knowledge gives him strength and encouragement for his avodah.
Rosh Hashana is the root of the whole year, so one must cry out 'HaMelech' on it so strongly that it is heard all year.
The shofar is the voice of a Jew's innermost self, a language only Hashem understands, which returns to Him the breath of life He blew into man.

title.en: Blessing in galus; Rosh Hashana and man's creation

summary.en: In a badly garbled opening the Rav speaks of blessing: in the time of the Mikdash the kohanim were given the task of blessing Israel, while in galus Hashem Himself, as it were, blesses them. He then turns to Rosh Hashana as the day man was created, the purpose of creation, when the angels were told to ask Israel when Rosh Hashana falls.

title.en: David and Shmuel find the place of the Mikdash

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that David sat with Shmuel in Ramah to determine the place of the Beis HaMikdash, and the Ramban that Hashem left it for Israel to find. They sought the highest place in the world from the borders in Sefer Yehoshua and found Ein Eitam, but placed the Mikdash twenty-three amos lower so that water from Ein Eitam could reach the mikveh.

title.en: Three heads: the king's soul, the Mikdash, Rosh Hashana

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew's soul is a letter of the Torah, and the general soul of Israel, the king's soul, corresponds to the beis of Bereishis that contains the whole Torah. So too the place of the Mikdash is the head of all places and Rosh Hashana the head of all times, all three tied to 'Bereishis'.

title.en: Why only David could reveal the place

summary.en: The Rav explains that the laws of the Beis HaMikdash are David's own portion in the Torah, since his soul, like Adam's and Moshiach's, is the root soul of Israel. Only the king could reveal the place of the Mikdash, and this, not ordinary scholarship, is why Doeg could not find what David found from the same verses.

title.en: A lowered Mikdash; Elul and Tishrei

summary.en: The Rav links the lowering of the Mikdash below the highest point to the humility a king must have, as seen in Shaul and David. In a heavily garbled stretch he then speaks of Rosh Hashana as Yom HaZikaron, of Elul and the days of selichos as the preparation for it, and of Tishrei's tie to the tribe of Ephraim.

title.en: Erev Rosh Hashana and 'Atem Nitzavim'

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that tzaddikim fast on erev Rosh Hashana, and the Midrash on 'Atem nitzavim' that all stand equal before Hashem. He then reads the verse 'your heads, your tribes ... from the hewer of your wood to the drawer of your water' and asks what the last phrase means, since it does not run from greatest to smallest.

title.en: All generations as one body

summary.en: The Rav brings the Tanya that, as a person has head, eyes and feet, so a generation has its heads and its lower members, and so too all generations together form one complete body: Moshe's generation is the head and the last generations are the heels. Compared with the great generations of the past, he says, ours seems to be nothing.

title.en: The test of serving in darkness

summary.en: The Rav contrasts earlier generations, who saw open wonders, with today's hidden faith, which is emunah precisely because one does not see. He explains the test of the Akeidah as going without understanding, brings the Or HaChaim that people would go mad for Torah if they felt its sweetness, and says the test of the last generations is to cling to Torah and serve Hashem without clarity; this is why the Akeidah is read on Rosh Hashana.

title.en: Hewers of wood and drawers of water

summary.en: The Rav explains that 'Atem nitzavim hayom' speaks to all the generations together: the last two levels, hewer of wood and drawer of water, are the last generations, for whom learning and davening are like chopping wood and drawing water. Moshe tells them they are all equal before Hashem, perhaps even more precious, and adds 'and with those who are not here with us today' so that no one would think he meant the order within one generation.

title.en: Knowing one's worth; who fasts erev Rosh Hashana

summary.en: The Rav says a person must know his strength and his worth before Hashem, because that gives him the will to toil in learning and davening, which today requires more effort. He explains why the Midrash allowed only tzaddikim to fast on erev Rosh Hashana while later poskim speak of everyone, even children, fasting: today's simple Jews, who kept believing through the Holocaust and hester panim, are as precious as the great ones of old.

title.en: The root of the year and the Lechovitcher's 'HaMelech'

summary.en: The Rav reads 'lest there be among you a root bearing gall and wormwood' as Moshe's warning to the generation of the wilderness, the head of all generations, whose slightest flaw could become real idolatry in later generations. Rosh Hashana, the root of the year, carries the same responsibility. He tells of a Lechovitcher chassid who heard his Rebbe's cry of 'HaMelech' from far away, and the Rebbe's words that the king's word must be heard throughout his kingdom.

title.en: The shofar: a voice only Hashem understands

summary.en: The Rav brings that 'shoresh poreh rosh' hints at the shofar, which can uproot even a bad root and bring back the most cast-away souls, and that our small shofar awakens the great shofar of Moshiach. The shofar returns to Hashem the breath of life He blew into man; all year one davens in words, but on Rosh Hashana with a sound from the inner self that only Hashem, who 'understands and listens', can read, like the jeweler with his loupe or the king who knew his lost son's cry.

title.en: Ashamed before the Avos within

summary.en: The Rav brings Reb Shlomo of Karlin that at the shofar one must be ashamed before the Avos, and explains that every Jew carries Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov within him. The teshuvah of Rosh Hashana is to feel the G-dly point inside oneself, to have mercy on it, and to know that a prince, precious to Hashem even in his lowly state, can serve Him in every situation.

title.en: A new yetzer tov; Rabbeinu Yonah's teshuvah

summary.en: The Rav brings Reb Pinchas's question on Tosafos, that the shofar confuses the Satan though he has heard it for thousands of years, and his answer that each year there is a new Satan; the Rav adds that each year Hashem then creates a new yetzer tov. He tells how Rabbeinu Yonah did teshuvah and wrote on it, urges learning his short Yesod HaTeshuvah before Rosh Hashana, and speaks of davening on the second day for one's own needs and for one's friends.

title.en: Reb Yosef Chaim's shidduch and a closing tefillah

summary.en: The Rav tells of Reb Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld, who accepted every shidduch proposed for his children except one, because on the previous Rosh Hashana he had not davened for that child's shidduch. He says one must daven on Rosh Hashana for every spiritual and material need, reflects on the hard year that passed, and closes asking Hashem for a new yetzer tov and for Moshiach.

catalogTitle: פרשה של אמונה. עשי"ת - זמן לנקות חציצות האמונה

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches that Parshas Haazinu, which contains everything that will happen to the Jewish people, is the parsha of emunah, and that the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah are the time to strengthen that emunah, daven with it and accept Hashem as King.

abstract.en: The Rav explains that Haazinu is read between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur because, like Rosh Hashanah for the year, it contains the whole Torah and all that will happen. He brings the Ramban that Haazinu promises the redemption with no condition of teshuvah, and that all its words have come true. From Haazinu he answers those who ask why the Jews of Europe did not resist, and he reads recent events and the failure of peace efforts in its light. Haazinu is called a song because with emunah even bitter decrees are known to come from Hashem. He stresses davening with emunah and answering amen in the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, and describes Rosh Hashanah as the day of gathering, when each Jew reaches the point of yechidah and makes Hashem King. He closes with a call to daven with mercy for the Jewish people.

en: Haazinu contains the whole Torah and everything that will happen, which is why it is read in the days that, like Rosh Hashanah, contain the whole year.
According to the Ramban, Haazinu promises the redemption without any condition of teshuvah, and everything it foretells has come true.
Haazinu is a song because emunah shows that everything, even what is bitter, comes from Hashem, and so it cannot be bad.
The success of the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah depends on davening with emunah, as if one saw the Judge writing the year's decree.
Not answering amen is a lack of emunah that prolongs the galus, which explains the severe language about talking during chazaras hashatz.
Rosh Hashanah is a day of gathering: all days gather to their head and all souls to their root, and each Jew must reach the innermost point of yechidah.
A Jew who makes Hashem King over all his thoughts, words and deeds is the switch that reveals Hashem's kingship over the whole world.

redemption and the end of days

title.en: Haazinu holds the whole Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that each Shabbos draws its influences from its parsha, and that Haazinu falls between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur because it includes everything. He tells how the Ramban showed a student his name hinted in Haazinu, and shows from the mitzvah of writing a Sefer Torah, learned from 'write for yourselves this song', that Haazinu contains the whole Torah.

title.en: The Ramban: a promise with no condition

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban that Haazinu contains no condition of teshuvah: it foretells the suffering, then vengeance on the enemies and the redemption, so that the nations will not say the world is not run by Hashem. With the Sifri he adds the Ramban's point that even if a stargazer had written this song one would have to believe it, since every word of it has come true.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah, the head of the year

summary.en: From 'He tells the end from the beginning' the Rav compares Haazinu to Rosh Hashanah: like the first letter of a word, Rosh Hashanah holds the whole year in potential, so not a minute of it may be lost. He speaks of the great events of the past year, tells R' Nosson Wachtfogel's mashal of a long-delayed wedding to show that the redemption is close, and ties the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah to the ten utterances of creation.

title.en: Why did they not resist?

summary.en: The Rav takes up a question bachurim brought to him: why did thousands of Jews in Europe let themselves be led to the gas chambers without resisting? He answers from Haazinu, 'how could one chase a thousand' unless 'their Rock sold them': Hashem handed them over. Haazinu also promises vengeance for the spilled blood and says it is near, and the Rav brings 'see now that I, I am He'.

title.en: A tradition: no peace before Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav describes a manuscript he has of traditions from chassidic gedolim, recorded with the name of each teller as the Russian chassidim did. From it he brings that before Moshiach every nation will want to rule the world, and a teaching in the name of the Apter Rav that the nations will see war does not help and will want peace, but will be dragged back and not allowed to make it. He applies this to the failed peace efforts of his day.

title.en: Miracles of our days and the true redemption

summary.en: The Rav reads Haazinu's verses of vengeance as what must happen before Moshiach, and laments that we are too small to grasp the great miracles of our days. He sees a blessing of Bechukosai fulfilled in recent events, when the enemies fought one another and no Jew was harmed. He brings the Rizhiner that the redemption will come through nature, yet stresses that the present government in Eretz Yisrael is not what Jews wait for: Moshiach is as the Rambam describes him, and anything else is a cheap imitation, though it may be a preparation.

title.en: Why Haazinu is called a song

summary.en: The Rav asks why Haazinu is called a song when most of it tells of bitter things. To answer, he brings the Sfas Emes on why Rosh Hashanah speaks constantly of judgment: Jews love Hashem so much that they want to be judged by Him, like a child who runs to his mother even if she will slap him. It is a great merit that Hashem remembers us, and this is why the day is called Yom HaZikaron.

title.en: Emunah turns the decree into song

summary.en: Following the Ramban, the Rav says Haazinu teaches emunah, and brings a segulah of saying Haazinu every day for emunah. Since Haazinu shows there is no chance and every Jew's whole life is written there by Hashem, what comes can be bitter but not bad, like a bitter but excellent wine that only an expert appreciates. Neither the White House nor the Kremlin writes the destiny of the world, and so Haazinu is a song of joy.

title.en: The shofar and its hundred sounds

summary.en: The Rav brings a responsum of the Rambam describing how he trembled on the bimah when he remembered Who commanded the shofar. The shofar is Hashem's message to the Jewish people; its hundred sounds correspond to the ten utterances of creation, each made of ten, with the first tekiah before them all. He returns to Haazinu: unlike other sidros it ends with harsh verses, because with emunah all of it is a song.

title.en: Davening with emunah and answering amen

summary.en: The Rav says the success of the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah depends on davening with emunah, as if one saw the Judge writing the year's decree, and Haazinu is the revelation of emunah. From 'children in whom there is no faith', which the Midrash reads as those who do not answer amen, he explains the severe words of the Shulchan Aruch about talking during chazaras hashatz, and brings R' Elchonon Wasserman that every minute of galus is pikuach nefesh, so one who does not answer amen prolongs it.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah, the day of gathering

summary.en: The Rav explains why chassidim went to great lengths to be with their Rebbe on Rosh Hashanah: it is a day of gathering and friendship, as in 'yom teruah'. Following Sefer Yetzirah's world, year and soul, all the days of the year gather to their head and all souls gather to their root. The shofar calls them together like a shepherd's horn, as in 'and the lost ones will come… and bow down on the holy mountain in Yerushalayim'.

title.en: The point of yechidah and Malchiyos

summary.en: In galus each Jew must find the holy mountain within himself: the innermost point of the soul, yechidah, where all Jewish souls are one with Hashem, and this is the avodah from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur. Malchiyos opens with Aleinu, said by Yehoshua when the walls of Yericho fell, because one must break the wall in one's heart. The Rav tells of a Lechovitcher chassid lost in a forest on Rosh Hashanah, and explains that a Jew who makes Hashem King over himself is the switch for the whole world.

title.en: Rebbi and the calf

summary.en: The Rav reports from a letter what a tzaddik said when hostages were taken: Rebbi suffered for thirteen years because he did not show mercy to a calf fleeing the slaughter. To the question why Yom Kippur did not atone, the answer is that this is not a matter of sin but of reality: as a person acts with mercy, so Hashem acts with him. From here the Rav says one must have great mercy on Jews in danger.

title.en: A call to daven with mercy

summary.en: The Rav urges not to forget, in the days of judgment, to daven with mercy for the Jewish people and Eretz Yisrael: our mercy is the master key that opens all locked gates. He closes with a tefillah that Hashem bring the redemption and fulfill the other blessing of Bechukosai, so that Jews may sing a song not only over suffering but over good.

catalogTitle: An Explanation of טומאת יולדת and מצוות מילה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains why a woman becomes tamei after giving birth, as the emptying of a great kedushah, and why Eliyahu HaNavi's coming to the bris on the eighth day cuts her tumah short after a boy.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Shabbos Rosh Chodesh Iyar, where the end of the week and the beginning of the month meet, and tells the story of Avner, the Ramban's student who went astray, to show that a Jew keeps his beginning and his end and can never be lost. He describes Sefirah as seven weeks of purifying the seven middos, part of a pattern of seven days of preparation and an eighth of purity that runs through the parshiyos. He then asks why a mother becomes tamei after giving birth, and why the Torah mentions milah there. Using the Ohr HaChaim's explanation of why a Jewish body is metamei b'ohel, he answers that the kedushah of the child who learned Torah in the womb has left her. To explain why a boy brings only seven days, he brings Eliyahu HaNavi, who comes to every bris and whose purity reaches the mother. He closes with Rosh Chodesh, Iyar as a time of renewal, and the call to fix one's middos and guard against lashon hara, which keeps Klal Yisrael out of Yerushalayim.

en: Shabbos Rosh Chodesh joins the kedushah of the end (Shabbos) with the kedushah of the beginning (Rosh Chodesh), while Amalek has only a beginning and no end.
A Jewish soul can never be lost forever; even Avner, who strayed, was hinted only in the middle letters of the words, keeping his beginning and his end.
Sefirah is a time of purifying the seven middos, and the parshiyos of these weeks repeat the pattern of seven days of preparation and purity on the eighth.
A mother becomes tamei after birth because the great kedushah of the child she carried has left her, just as the Ohr HaChaim explains why a Jewish body is metamei b'ohel.
After a boy the tumah lasts only seven days because Eliyahu HaNavi comes to the bris on the eighth day, and his purity reaches the mother as a close relative.
Iyar, the month of Tazria-Metzora, is a time to repair one's middos between man and his fellow and to guard against lashon hara, which turned Klal Yisrael into a metzora sent out of Yerushalayim.

title.en: Shabbos Rosh Chodesh: beginning and end

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the double parsha and of Rosh Chodesh Iyar as a capsule of the whole month and a time of renewal, like the moon reborn. When Rosh Chodesh falls on Shabbos the kedushah of the end and of the beginning join, while Amalek has only a beginning.

title.en: Avner, the Ramban's student

summary.en: The Rav tells the story from the mussar sefarim of Avner, a student of the Ramban who became an apikores and an officer of the king, summoned the Ramban on Yom Kippur, and was shown his name in the third letters of a passuk in Ha'azinu.

title.en: Why a Jew can never be lost

summary.en: The Rav asks why Avner was hinted in the middle letters, when only the first and last letters of a word contain the whole word. He answers that a Jewish soul is never lost forever: Avner lost only his middle and kept his beginning and his end, unlike Amalek.

title.en: Sefirah: seven to purify, the eighth to be pure

summary.en: The Rav explains Sefirah as cleansing the seven middos (chesed, gevurah, tiferes), seven times seven, before Matan Torah. He shows the same pattern of seven and the eighth in Shemini, in the yoledes, in the metzora, and in shemittah and yovel.

title.en: Two questions on the yoledes

summary.en: The Rav asks why the passuk about a mother's tumah mentions milah on the eighth day, and why she becomes tamei at all after bringing a Jewish child into the world, a child who learned the whole Torah from a malach in the womb.

title.en: The Ohr HaChaim's honey can

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ohr HaChaim, who asks why a Jewish body is metamei b'ohel and a non-Jew's is not, and answers with the mashal of flies swarming an emptied honey can: tumah feeds on the residue of kedushah. The Rav applies this to the mother who carried a 'beis medrash' within her.

title.en: Eliyahu at the bris cuts the tumah short

summary.en: The Rav asks why a boy, whose kedushah in the womb is greater, brings seven days of tumah and a girl fourteen. Showing that a close relative shares both the din of an avel and the simchah of a bris, he answers that Eliyahu HaNavi, connected to the eighth and free of tumah, comes to the bris and his purity interrupts the mother's tumah.

title.en: Shavuos as the eighth, Rosh Chodesh and Iyar

summary.en: The Rav returns to Sefirah as days of taharah leading to Shavuos, the eighth, like yovel after seven times seven. He explains Rosh Chodesh as the moon's renewed union with the sun, a special Yom Tov for women, connected to Rachel and Dovid HaMelech, and Iyar as the month of renewal in ruchniyus and in nature.

title.en: Middos, lashon hara and the return to Yerushalayim

summary.en: The Rav ties Tazria-Metzora to Sefirah as days of fixing middos between man and his fellow, recalls the students of Rabbi Akiva, and warns against lashon hara, which makes a metzora and drove Klal Yisrael out of Yerushalayim. He brings the Gemara of Mashiach as a metzora at the gates of Rome and ends that the real battle is fought in the batei medrash.

catalogTitle: פרשה שכולל הכל - מכוון כנגד עשי"ת שכולל הכל

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Parshas Haazinu, which contains the whole Torah and every Jewish soul, is read on Shabbos Shuvah, the Shabbos that contains the whole year, and builds from it the path of emunah, malchus and closeness to Hashem through the Ten Days of Teshuvah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Bnei Yissaschar's advice to say Haazinu daily as a segulah for emunah, and explains that every Jew has hidden emunah which the Ten Days of Teshuvah uncover by removing chatzitzos, with Yom Kippur as a mikveh. Following the Ramban, Haazinu is a written testimony: since its earlier prophecies came true, the promised redemption, which has no condition of teshuvah, must come too. Because the mitzvah of writing a Sefer Torah is learned from writing Haazinu, Haazinu contains the whole Torah and every Jewish soul, as the story of the Ramban and his student Avner shows; the Rav explains why Avner was hinted in the middle letters. Shabbos Shuvah, which contains all the Shabbosos of the year, therefore reads Haazinu. He then speaks of the disappointment over the year 5736, the Arizal and hidden beginnings of redemption, malchiyos on Rosh Hashanah, and Yom Kippur as Hashem speaking to His children as a Father.

en: Every Jew has emunah inside him; mitzvos and answering amen draw it out, and the Ten Days of Teshuvah remove the chatzitzos that cover it.
According to the Ramban, Haazinu is a testimony with no condition of teshuvah: what it foretold has come true, so the redemption it promises must come as well.
Since the mitzvah to write a Sefer Torah is learned from the command to write Haazinu, Haazinu contains the whole Torah, and with it every Jewish soul.
Shabbos Shuvah contains all the Shabbosos and days of the year, so on it one reads Haazinu, the small parsha that contains all the sedros and all souls.
On Rosh Hashanah Hashem is crowned as King and seen from afar; on Yom Kippur He speaks to the Jew as a Father, Avinu Malkeinu, washing away his sins.

title.en: Haazinu, amen and hidden emunah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar's advice to say Haazinu daily as a segulah for emunah, explains that answering amen and the mitzvos draw out the emunah hidden in every Jew, and that the Ten Days of Teshuvah remove its chatzitzos, with Yom Kippur as a mikveh.

title.en: Haazinu as a testimony that contains the whole Torah

summary.en: Following the Ramban, the Rav explains that Haazinu is a testimony without any condition of teshuvah: what it foretold came true, so the redemption must come. He then shows from the mitzvah of writing a Sefer Torah, learned from writing Haazinu, that Haazinu contains the whole Torah.

title.en: The Ramban and his student Avner

summary.en: Since every Jew is a letter of the Torah, every soul is in Haazinu. The Rav tells the story of the Ramban's student Avner, who doubted this, and was shown his name in the third letters of a passuk in Haazinu.

title.en: Why Avner was hinted in the middle letters

summary.en: The Rav asks why the hint was in the third letters and not in the first or last. He explains that a Jew's root and end can never be erased, as no one is cast away forever; only the middle, a temporary state, can be.

title.en: Shabbos Shuvah contains the whole year

summary.en: Each of the seven days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur repairs that weekday for the whole year, and Shabbos Shuvah contains all of the year's Shabbosos; therefore it reads Haazinu, which contains all the sedros and souls. He then speaks of the disappointment felt when Rosh Hashanah came and the year 5736 passed without redemption.

title.en: The Arizal, mazal and the Megillah's hidden start

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Arizal could not know when Moshiach comes, but saw that the mazal of 5736 was suited for it. From the Megillah, whose miracle began long before it became visible, he suggests that the redemption may already have begun unseen.

title.en: Waiting for the mechutan; the Ba'al Shem Tov and the rider

summary.en: The Rav tells Rabbi Nosson Wachtfogel's story of an older chassan whose wedding had begun while all waited for the mechutan, and the Ba'al Shem Tov's story of a man born to be king whose mazal was fulfilled by riding a horse to applause. He suggests the mazal of 5736 may have been fulfilled through the rescue at Uganda.

title.en: Malchiyos: breaking the walls and crowning the King within

summary.en: Malchiyos begins with Aleinu, which was said at the walls of Yericho; accepting Hashem's kingship breaks the walls between a Jew and Hashem, through Hoshana Rabbah and Shemini Atzeres. Since man is a small world, the Rav stresses accepting malchus on oneself, which then spreads it over the whole world.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah is Malkeinu, Yom Kippur Avinu Malkeinu

summary.en: On Rosh Hashanah the people ask the King to show Himself; on Yom Kippur Hashem washes His children as a parent does. The Rav explains why the middle brachah of Yom Kippur alone contains pesukim: in Torah Hashem speaks to us, and on Yom Kippur He speaks as a Father, calling the Jew to return.

title.en: The sweetness of Yom Kippur and the light of these days

summary.en: The Rav explains that one does not eat on Yom Kippur because physicality is a chatzitzah to dveikus, and that every moment of the day should be savored. He compares the special light of these days to the light of Shabbos candles, tells of Rabbi Avraham Kalisker's answer to a fundraising proposal during the Ten Days, and closes with a blessing.

catalogTitle: דיבורים המעוררים את הלב

oneLiner.en: For Elul, the Rav teaches that releasing others as in shmitah brings Hashem's release of our debts, and warns that letzanus, the scoffing that undoes emunah, shut Pharaoh off from reality and shuts a person out of tefillah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Elul as the forty days of favor when Moshe went up for the second luchos, and says the teshuvah of that time left its mark on the season for all generations. From the parsha of shmitah he explains that shmitah means letting go: what a person does below, Hashem does above, so one who releases what others owe him causes Hashem to release his own debt. This happens each Tishrei and, in small, every Shabbos, and is why one makes peace with others before Rosh Hashanah and accepts love of one's fellow before davening. Strengthening each other is the call of the time, and its great enemy is letzanus. With Rabbi Tzadok he shows that letzanus is the opposite of emunah and shuts a person out of the palaces of tefillah. Pharaoh, a scoffer, used jokes to escape the reality of the plagues, and was punished measure for measure. He closes with Rosh Hashanah as a day of emes and with Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael.

en: The forty days of Elul were days of favor, and the teshuvah Klal Yisrael did then left a lasting mark on the season for all generations.
Shmitah means letting go; when a person releases what others owe him, Hashem correspondingly releases the debt of his sins.
Elul calls for strengthening one another in serving Hashem, and letzanus is what most cools a person's Yiddishkeit.
Following Rabbi Tzadok, emunah is the root and entrance of all good and letzanus is the root of all bad and the entrance to the opposite.
A scoffer is pushed away from the palaces of tefillah and loses his connection to davening and learning.
Pharaoh withstood the plagues because, as a scoffer, he used jokes to escape reality, and Hashem punished him measure for measure by making sport of Egypt.

title.en: Elul, the days of favor and the second luchos

summary.en: The Rav describes the forty days of favor when Moshe went up for the second luchos and the broken spirit of the people after the egel, and says their teshuvah left a mark on these days for all generations. He adds that the second luchos were given to baalei teshuvah and were greater than the first.

title.en: Shmitah and the beloved seventh

summary.en: From the parsha of shmitah the Rav explains that shmitah means letting go, and that every mitzvah a person does below Hashem does correspondingly above. He brings that every seventh is beloved, Shabbos among days and Tishrei among months, and notes that the shmitah cycle of years begins from Tishrei.

title.en: Releasing others' debts before Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem gave the mitzvah of releasing debts so that by letting go of what others owe us we arouse Him to let go of our own debt, and that this happens every Tishrei and every Shabbos, a small Rosh Hashanah. He brings the Gemara that the Satan has no power on Yom Kippur, and speaks of being mochel others and accepting love of one's fellow before davening in Elul.

title.en: Letzanus, the opposite of emunah

summary.en: The Rav calls for strengthening one another in serving Hashem and warns that letzanus cools a person's Yiddishkeit. With Rabbi Tzadok he explains that emunah, the first of the Ten Commandments, is the root and entrance of all good, while letzanus is the root of all bad, and that Heaven helps the scoffer in his scoffing.

title.en: Scoffers shut out of the palaces of tefillah

summary.en: The Rav describes how a bochur who davens with warmth is mocked, and calls letzanus the kelipah of Amalek. He brings the Gemara that scoffers do not receive the Shechinah, and Rabbi Tzadok's explanation that a scoffer is not let into the palaces of tefillah, comparing it to the guards placed at Gan Eden and to the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that a person is where his thoughts are, with a story of the Ba'al Shem Tov.

title.en: Pharaoh the scoffer

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that calls Pharaoh a letz and asks where Pharaoh's scoffing is seen, and why a logical man kept withstanding plague after plague. He answers that jokes are an escape from reality, and illustrates how one joke silences a hundred rebukes with a story of a child who ended a derashah about the Leviasan.

title.en: Pharaoh's punishment, measure for measure

summary.en: The Rav brings the passuk 'that I made sport of Egypt' with Rashi's explanation, and says Pharaoh's punishment was measure for measure: Hashem made a joke of the one who made jokes. He then describes how Yosef gathered the world's money into Egypt, the envy of the nations, and how it all went out with Yosef's family.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah as a day of emes

summary.en: Much of this stretch is lost in the recording. In what survives, the Rav calls the theme the preparation for Rosh Hashanah, points to the conclusion of the Rosh Hashanah brachah, which speaks of emes, and says that since the Torah binds every Jew, each one must make a cheshbon for himself.

title.en: Elul and Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael

summary.en: In a poorly recorded closing, the Rav says that just as Moshe began in Elul to bring the luchos down from heaven, a Jew must now purify his heart and bind himself to Hashem, mentions 'one thing I ask of Hashem', and speaks of the great love between Hashem and a Jew, for which a person gives everything he has. He ends with wishes for a good Elul and a good Rosh Hashanah.

catalogTitle: לדוד ה' אורי - בבטחון תלוי הכל

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Elul is a city of refuge that must be signposted and used, that the Arizal's promise for saying L'Dovid Hashem Ori depends on living with its message of bitachon, and that the forty days are a mikveh in which a person must above all repair his middos toward others.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Bnei Yissaschar: the verse about the accidental killer, whose initials spell Elul, shows that Elul is a city of refuge from the yetzer hara. Just as the Torah demands signs pointing to the refuge, Elul must be made known, for its path is a road through the sea, easily lost. He laments that the fear of Elul felt in earlier generations is gone. He then brings the Arizal's promise that whoever says L'Dovid Hashem Ori from Rosh Chodesh Elul is assured a good judgment, and explains that, like Ashrei, it works only through living its content: bitachon, which touches every area of avodah. Through Rashi he shows the heart carries Hashem's message in Elul. The forty days are a mikveh of forty se'ah, every hour a lug. Finally he stresses bein adam lachaveiro, with Rabbi Yisrael Salanter's story, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's teaching, and the Malbim's story.

en: Elul is a city of refuge, and like the Torah's signs at the crossroads it must be pointed out so that people actually flee into it.
The Arizal's promise for saying L'Dovid Hashem Ori is fulfilled only when one takes its message of bitachon to heart, as with the Gemara's promise for Ashrei.
Bitachon decides practical conduct: coming to shul, guarding the eyes, not talking before davening or in the mikveh, and not interrupting learning for news.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are a mikveh of forty se'ah, and each of their 960 hours is one lug.
Elul calls above all for teshuvah on middos and bein adam lachaveiro, since shaming another is a form of shedding blood.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's teaching that Yom Kippur does not atone for sins against another points at what must be fixed, which is why Ne'ilah focuses on the wrong done to others.

title.en: Elul as a city of refuge

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the initials of 'ina l'yado v'samti lach' spell Elul, making Elul a refuge from the yetzer hara, and connects it to the command to prepare the road with signs to the refuge. He explains the month's verse, 'a road in the sea', as a path on which one can easily stray and let the days slip by.

title.en: The lost awe of Elul

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the fear that seized Jews when Elul came, as described in older seforim, with today's indifference, and protests against scheduling outings on the days of Rosh Chodesh Elul. He concludes that one must strengthen oneself and look for the signs on the road to Hashem.

title.en: The Arizal's promise for L'Dovid

summary.en: The Rav reads the Arizal's tradition, brought in the siddur of Rabbi Shabsai, that saying L'Dovid Hashem Ori from Rosh Chodesh Elul until after Simchas Torah assures a good year, and asks how mere recital can guarantee this. Comparing Ashrei and Parshas HaMan, he answers that one must live with the chapter's content, which is bitachon, and shows bitachon with the Gemara about one who misses shul.

title.en: Bitachon in everyday avodah

summary.en: The Rav applies bitachon to guarding the eyes on the street, not speaking before davening, not speaking in the mikveh, and not breaking off learning to hear news. In each case, he says, the excuse that one might lose something is answered by bitachon.

title.en: Inside L'Dovid: bitachon and the heart's message

summary.en: The Rav goes through verses of L'Dovid to show the whole chapter is bitachon, and explains that one who relies only on Hashem is judged by Hashem alone. With Rashi on 'lecha amar libi' he explains that in Elul the heart is Hashem's messenger calling a Jew to seek Him, and with the Targum on 'l'maan shorerai' that a Jew wants a good year in order to sing to Hashem.

title.en: The forty days as a mikveh

summary.en: The Rav brings the Bnei Yissaschar that the forty days are forty se'ah and their 960 hours are 960 lugin of a mikveh, explaining why Rabbi Akiva's 'mikveh Yisrael Hashem' closes Yoma. He adds his own reading of a phrase in the Hoshanos about three hours, the repair of a mikveh through hashakah, and the Arizal's kavanah of 'lev tahor' at tevilah.

title.en: Elul and teshuvah on middos

summary.en: The Rav stresses that besides learning and davening one must work on middos in these forty days, citing the Rambam on teshuvah for character traits. He notes that Elul's verse speaks of a killer, and shaming another is a kind of bloodshed, and that the Elul verses the seforim bring all concern bein adam lachaveiro.

title.en: Rabbi Yisrael Salanter and the torn shoe

summary.en: The Rav tells how a man shamed a former shoemaker at his child's chuppah by handing him a torn shoe to price, and how Rabbi Yisrael Salanter said the rabbanim of Vilna must make an accounting. He adds that some rabbanim hold the destruction in Europe came because of corrupt middos, and that such ways must be uprooted.

title.en: 'This' Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah expounded

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Mishnah says 'this' Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah expounded, and explains that his generation, which saw the Churban, pointed a finger at sins between man and his fellow as its cause. He links it to the last moments of Yom Kippur, when Ne'ilah speaks only of the wrong done to others, including taking away what is due to them.

title.en: The Malbim and the Chasam Sofer's place

summary.en: The Rav tells the tradition from the Chasam Sofer's students of how the young Malbim stood in the Chasam Sofer's place, causing him distress, and from then on the gates of Torah closed for him, so that he wrote only on Tanach and spent every Shabbos at Minchah asking forgiveness. He closes with the Gemara that a learned person must make Hashem's Name beloved through pleasant dealings, and calls for teshuvah on middos.

catalogTitle: Understanding the Mistake of the מגדף and how it Pertains to ל”ג בעומר

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the megadef, the man who cursed Hashem's Name, denied that every Jew is a letter of the Sefer Torah and that Hashem's love for every shevet stays warm like the lechem hapanim, and that Lag BaOmer, the day of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, reveals this hidden worth of every Jew.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the lechem hapanim, twelve loaves each kneaded separately, and the megadef who, Rashi says, quarreled over his place in the camp of Dan and mocked the lechem hapanim. He explains that every Jew's soul is rooted in a letter of the Sefer Torah, and the camps in the desert were arranged like a Sefer Torah, so an outsider is like an extra letter. The megadef, an apikores whom the Arizal identifies with a later figure, argued that Dan was a rejected tribe. The answer is that no Jew is rejected: each loaf, for each tribe, matches one of the twelve arrangements of Hashem's Name, and the loaves stayed warm, like Hashem's love. Yechezkel after the first Churban, and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai after the second, revealed the hidden point in every Jew. This is the joy of Lag BaOmer, linked to Purim, a day of chizuk for even the lowest Jew.

en: Every Jew's soul is rooted in a letter of the Sefer Torah, and the camps in the desert were arranged so that the whole camp formed a Sefer Torah.
The tribe of Dan refused the megadef a place because an extra person in the camp is like an extra letter, which spoils a Sefer Torah.
Each of the twelve loaves of the lechem hapanim must be made separately because each corresponds to a tribe and to one of the twelve arrangements of Hashem's four-letter Name.
The lechem hapanim stayed warm for nine days to show that Hashem's warm love for every Jew, even the tribe of Dan, never cools.
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, by revealing the secrets of the Torah, revealed the hidden worth of every Jew, and this is the joy of Lag BaOmer.
Every Jew, even the lowest, has a unique quality no other Jew has, and recognizing it leads one to honor every other Jew.

title.en: The lechem hapanim and the megadef

summary.en: The Rav asks why each loaf of the lechem hapanim must be made separately, then brings Rashi that the megadef mocked the lechem hapanim and quarreled over his place in the camp of Dan. He describes the miracle that the loaves stayed warm for nine days and asks why the man cursed Hashem rather than the people who turned him away.

title.en: The camp of Israel as a Sefer Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew is rooted in a letter of the Sefer Torah, with Yisrael read as the initials of 600,000 letters, and that the camps and flags in the desert, with Levi in the middle like Vayikra among the five Chumashim, formed a Sefer Torah. He adds the four camps of the angels, the Midrash on 'shuvi shuvi', and why the counting had to be by names.

title.en: An extra letter spoils the Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Dan refused the megadef because an extra letter, like a missing one, disqualifies a Sefer Torah. He brings the Arizal that the megadef was an apikores later reincarnated as Yeshu, and that he scoffed at the idea of the camps; they answered him with the twelve loaves that correspond to the twelve tribes.

title.en: Dan, the lowest tribe, is not rejected

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Dan is the lowest tribe, notes its idol worship and Shlomis bas Divri, and presents the megadef's claim that Dan is rejected anyway. The reply is that no Jew is rejected, and the proof is that each loaf is kneaded separately because each tribe is one of the twelve arrangements of Hashem's Name, as the siddur lists them for each month.

title.en: The Arizal's zemer and the warm loaves

summary.en: The Rav brings the Arizal's Shabbos zemer, which asks Hashem to reveal the secret of the twelve loaves, and explains that the secret is the depth of the Jewish soul. Hashem's warm love for every tribe is shown by the loaves staying warm, while the megadef insisted that the loaves were cold and stale.

title.en: The claim that the love has cooled

summary.en: The Rav ties the megadef's two complaints into one: if the loaves are cold, the love for Dan has cooled, which he calls the whole teaching of Yeshu. Against this he says Hashem is warm to every Jew, who is a letter of the Torah, and that the Torah has four levels, Pardes; the Arizal says one who denies its secrets is like an animal.

title.en: Yechezkel and Rabbi Shimon in exile

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that Yechezkel's vision of the Merkavah, read as the haftarah of Shavuos, came to encourage the exiles who thought Hashem had rejected them. After the second Churban, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai did the same by revealing the secrets of the Torah: there is a hidden point in every Jew, even the greatest rasha, that never leaves Hashem.

title.en: Honoring every Jew's hidden quality

summary.en: The Rav explains that Rabbi Akiva's students did not honor each other because they did not see that every Jew has a quality no other has, without which the Sefer Torah is incomplete. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai taught this, and the Rav brings the sefer Beis Aharon that Rabbi Shimon is for everyone, even the lowest, and Rabbi Akiva's 'love your fellow as yourself'.

title.en: The joy of Lag BaOmer

summary.en: The Rav explains that Lag BaOmer, which falls in hod, the trait of bending oneself to every Jew, ends the mourning of the sefirah. Every Jew, even the lowest, feels uplifted on that day, as seen in the great joy of all kinds of Jews in Meron, because the soul feels that Rabbi Shimon revealed its importance to Hashem.

title.en: Lag BaOmer, Purim and chizuk

summary.en: The Rav links Lag BaOmer to Purim through the calendar sign that Lag BaOmer falls on the weekday of Purim: both are for those who stumbled, the tribe of Dan whom Amalek attacked. He concludes that Parshas Emor with its twelve loaves comes before Lag BaOmer to teach that Hashem's love never cools, and that every Jew should take chizuk from Rabbi Shimon.

catalogTitle: אלול ור"ה בזמן מכוון כנגד ירושלים ובהמ"ק במקום (שייכות לפרשת שופטים)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that just as the Beis Hamikdash is the central point of place from which creation began, Elul, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are the central point of time, and like the place Hashem chose, they must be sought.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the parsha of the Great Sanhedrin in Parshas Shoftim and asks why, in so vital a parsha, the Torah tells that the Beis Hamikdash is higher than all places. He contrasts the exact location given for Har Grizim with the unnamed place Hashem will choose, which must be sought. He explains that place, time and soul each have a central point: the Mikdash, where creation began and Creator meets creation; the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur, the forming of the year; and the Sanhedrin and its greatest sage. A small point contains the whole, as Rosh Hashanah contains the year. This explains 'makom gorem' for the rebellious elder, whose pasuk is the middle pasuk of Devarim. Like Dovid and Avraham, one must search for Rosh Hashanah, ask friends and elders the way, and, as his advice, learn mussar every day.

en: Place, time and soul each have a central point from which they develop: the Beis Hamikdash, Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and the Great Sanhedrin with its greatest sage.
The Mikdash is 'higher than all places' because it is the point where Hashem began creation and where the Creator is in contact with the creation, not because it is physically the highest.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are the formation period of the year, like the forty days in which a child is formed, when prayer can still shape what it will be.
The Torah does not name the place of the Mikdash so that it be sought, and in the same way Rosh Hashanah must be sought by climbing the mountain from Rosh Chodesh Elul.
A small point can contain the whole: Rosh Hashanah contains the year as the head contains the body.
As his advice for keeping Rosh Hashanah through the year, the Rav says to take on learning mussar every day, even for ten minutes.
