title.en: Why the Torah says the Mikdash is highest

summary.en: The Rav opens with the parsha of the Great Sanhedrin and the derashah that the Beis Hamikdash is higher than all places. He brings the Ramban that this parsha is a great foundation, since without it every person would explain the Torah his own way, and asks why so vital a parsha includes what seems a minor point of geography.

title.en: The chosen place must be sought

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the exact location the Torah gives for Har Grizim and Har Eival with the unnamed 'place Hashem will choose'. With the Ramban and the Sifrei on 'lishchno sidreshu' he explains that the place must be searched for, with people asking one another the way, and only afterwards does a navi confirm it, as happened with Dovid.

title.en: The Mikdash as the center of creation

summary.en: The Rav explains that world, year and soul each have a central point. The Mikdash is the point from which Hashem began creating the world, like a weaver starting from a center, the place of contact between Creator and creation. He brings the Chasam Sofer citing the Kaftor vaFerach that Eretz Yisrael is not literally higher, and explains with a ball, whose highest point only its maker knows.

title.en: Jerusalem, the highest mountain

summary.en: The Rav explains that Jerusalem is not physically the highest mountain, yet it is the highest because creation began there, and in the end of days this will be seen by all, as the navi says the mountain of Hashem's house will stand at the head of the mountains and Torah will go out from Tzion. He compares this to the development of a child from a first point, as the Tanya brings.

title.en: The forty days of Elul form the year

summary.en: The Rav applies the idea to time: the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are the formation of the year, like the forty days in which a child is formed, when one can still pray for a blessed outcome. He brings the Ba'al HaTurim's gematria of zachar and berachah and the reading of 'Re'eh' on the Shabbos blessing Elul, and calls Elul the Eretz Yisrael of the year, the Ten Days its Yerushalayim, and Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur its central point.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah, the point of closeness

summary.en: The Rav explains that on Rosh Hashanah, as in the Mikdash, Hashem is close to creation, since each year the first Rosh Hashanah of creation repeats itself; this is 'Dirshu Hashem behimatzo'. As Shlomo planted every species in Jerusalem, the whole year grows from Rosh Hashanah, the head that contains the body. The climb to it begins at Rosh Chodesh Elul, a hard ascent to the source of all blessing, a small point containing much.

title.en: A small place holding much: Aron and Avos

summary.en: The Rav brings examples of a small thing holding much: Eretz Yisrael as 'Eretz Tzvi', and the Kodesh HaKodashim, where the Aron took up no space, a place above the rules of nature where Creator and creation unite. The forty-eight hours of Rosh Hashanah are such a point, and so are the Avos, called mountains, who were born in Tishrei.

title.en: The central point in the Torah

summary.en: The Rav says that whatever is in creation is in the Torah, since Hashem looked into the Torah like a builder into his plans and created the world, so the Torah too has a central point. He raises possibilities for where it is, mentions the dispute whether the world was created in Tishrei or Nisan without expanding, and adds that Sefer Devarim is a Torah of its own, a Mishneh Torah, as Tosafos at the beginning of Gittin indicates.

title.en: Makom gorem: the rebellious elder

summary.en: Returning to the parsha of the rebellious elder, the Rav brings the Gemara's derashah that 'the place causes': he is liable only when the Great Sanhedrin sits in its place in the Mikdash. He explains that the central soul, the Sanhedrin and its greatest sage, must sit in the central place from which Torah goes out to the world, and shows from the Masorah that the middle pasuk of Sefer Devarim is the pasuk of 'min hamakom hahu'.

title.en: The highest laws go to the highest place

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Mikdash is a hidden place above intellect and nature. Just as Jerusalem was not divided among the tribes, which had local courts for local laws, only the highest laws, those carrying kares, go up to the Great Sanhedrin and can make an elder rebellious; he ties this to tefillin, which are above the head, and to 'ki yipalei', the mufla.

title.en: Seeking Rosh Hashanah like Dovid

summary.en: The Rav applies 'lishchno sidreshu' to Rosh Hashanah: some reach the date but never find the day and do not hear its shofar. Like Dovid, who would not sleep until he found a place for Hashem, Jews rise in the night for Selichos in Elul. On Rosh Hashanah night they say 'Mi ya'aleh behar Hashem', and only one with clean hands who prepared ascends, just as entry to the Mikdash was graded by holiness.

title.en: Avraham's search and Elul's rashei teivos

summary.en: The Rav describes Avraham searching for the place at the Akeidah until Hashem showed it to him, and says Jerusalem, Rosh Hashanah and the Ten Days must likewise be sought. He explains why even simple halachah books bring the rashei teivos of Elul: a head contains the whole. With the Ramban, he says one must leave far-off interests and ask, 'Which is the way to Hashem's house?'

title.en: Asking friends and elders the way

summary.en: Continuing the Ramban on 'Lechu venaaleh el har Hashem', the Rav says one cannot prepare alone: one must speak with G-d-fearing friends and ask talmidei chachamim and elders how to reach Rosh Hashanah, since one Rosh Hashanah can decide many years, as with Yosef's seven years. He notes that resolutions from Rosh Hashanah usually fade within weeks.

title.en: Daily mussar, and closing blessings

summary.en: As his advice, the Rav says, citing the Mishnah Berurah, to take on learning mussar every day, even ten minutes, from a sefer that fits one's soul, especially foundational works like Chovos HaLevavos and Shaarei Teshuvah; this carries the shofar's call through the whole year. He urges not to lose a day of Elul, the 'yerach yamim', and closes with blessings for a good year and the great shofar of the redemption.

catalogTitle: בימי אלול אנו הולכים בדרך שמביא אותנו למקום מקדשינו בזמן - ראש השנה (שייכות לפרשת שופטים)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that just as a Jew brought bikkurim, the first fruits, up to the Beis HaMikdash, in Elul he travels toward Rosh Hashanah, the Beis HaMikdash in time, where he must arrive with joy in Hashem's kingship and with the freshness of a new beginning.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Nechemiah telling the weeping people on Rosh Hashanah to rejoice, and the Chasam Sofer's parable of a prisoner freed for rejoicing on the king's coronation day. He then asks why bikkurim, which began only after the land was settled, are called the merit for entering it, why the farmer recites Arami oved avi, and why the bikkurim procession was so festive. Yetzias Mitzrayim, he explains, draws Jews out even from the fiftieth gate, and the fiftieth mention of it in the Torah is in the bikkurim declaration. Bikkurim, the seven species standing for seven kinds of Jews, were a prophetic act foreshadowing the return to Yerushalayim. Rosh Hashanah is reishis, the Beis HaMikdash in time, which no churban could touch, and the Mikdash comes to every prepared Jew. He ends with Moshe's prayer, the freshness of the Mikdash, and a call to zrizus.

en: According to the Rav, rejoicing in Hashem's kingship on Rosh Hashanah, more than worry over one's own judgment, is itself the merit in judgment.
The fiftieth mention of yetzias Mitzrayim in the Torah, the one in praise of Israel, is the Arami oved avi declaration over bikkurim, and the future geulah lies hidden in it.
Bringing bikkurim from the seven species to Yerushalayim is a prophetic act (poel dimyoni) showing that Hashem will bring every kind of Jew back to Tziyon after the churban.
Rosh Hashanah is the reishis of time just as the Beis HaMikdash is the reishis of place; it is the Beis HaMikdash in time.
On Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur there is no aliyah l'regel because the Mikdash comes to every Jew wherever he is, provided he has prepared in Elul.
Time is above place, so the churban ruled only over the Mikdash of place, never over the Mikdash of time.
The Mikdash is the place of reishis and freshness where nothing grows old, and on Rosh Hashanah a Jew asks to keep that freshness in avodas Hashem all year.

candidateTopics: Rosh Hashanah as the Beis HaMikdash in time

title.en: Nechemiah and the king's coronation day

summary.en: The Rav opens with Nechemiah telling the weeping people on Rosh Hashanah to eat, drink and rejoice, and brings the Chasam Sofer's parable of a prisoner who danced on the king's coronation day and was pardoned. Rejoicing in Hashem's kingship, he explains, is a Jew's strength in judgment.

title.en: Questions on the parsha of bikkurim

summary.en: The Rav mentions the Chassidic custom of dancing on Rosh Hashanah and turns to the parsha of bikkurim. He asks how bikkurim can be the merit for entering the land when they began only after it was settled, why the farmer recounts yetzias Mitzrayim, and why the bikkurim procession was so festive; he also notes that the curses are read before Rosh Hashanah.

title.en: Arami oved avi and the fiftieth gate

summary.en: The Rav asks why Chazal fixed the mitzvah of telling yetzias Mitzrayim on the verses of Arami oved avi rather than on the fuller account in Shemos. He brings the Ohr HaChaim that Israel was taken out before falling into the fiftieth gate of impurity, while with the power of Torah one can come out even from there.

title.en: The Haggadah and the power of Torah

summary.en: The Rav connects this to the Haggadah: the blessing over the giving of the Torah is placed before the four sons, because the Torah can pull out even the rasha who has fallen into the fiftieth gate. He adds that yetzias Mitzrayim comes from the fifty gates of understanding and is mentioned fifty times in the Torah.

title.en: The fiftieth mention of yetzias Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav brings the question that yetzias Mitzrayim appears more than fifty times, and the answer that only fifty mentions are in praise of Israel. Counting back from the end of the Torah, he sets aside verses that do not count, and concludes that the fiftieth is the Arami oved avi declaration over bikkurim, where the key to the final geulah lies.

title.en: The seven species and the prophetic act

summary.en: The Rav explains the land of the seven species as the seven kinds of Jews, from wheat down to the pomegranate, the empty ones who are still full of mitzvos. He then introduces the poel dimyoni, an act that strengthens a prophecy, from the Ramban on Yaakov's bow and from Yirmiyahu buying a field before the churban.

title.en: Bikkurim as a sign of the return to Tziyon

summary.en: The Rav explains that bringing bikkurim of the seven species to the Mikdash is a poel dimyoni for the ingathering after the churban; this is why the procession had music and gilded horns, as the haftarah describes the geulah. Therefore the parsha of the fiftieth mention is read before Rosh Hashanah, whose tefillos ask above all for the geulah.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah, the Beis HaMikdash in time

summary.en: From the verse 'from the beginning of the year' said of Eretz Yisroel, the Rav explains that Eretz Yisroel, Yerushalayim and the Mikdash are the point of reishis in place, and Rosh Hashanah is the same point in time. Bikkurim are the reishis of the produce, so on Rosh Hashanah a Jew brings himself like bikkurim to the Mikdash, which he reaches through the days until Ne'ilah.

title.en: Elul's preparation and the joyful shofar

summary.en: The Rav says not everyone arrives at Tziyon when Rosh Hashanah comes; one must prepare in Elul with regret and correcting one's middos. The word vehaya means joy and the future, and one who prepared weeps on Rosh Hashanah like a child returning to his father, while the shofar becomes a song of Hashem's coronation and the Mikdash comes to him.

title.en: Repeated passage in the recording

summary.en: The recording replays the passage from the call to prepare for Tziyon through the Mikdash coming to every Jew almost word for word; it adds nothing to the preceding section.

title.en: No aliyah l'regel: time above place

summary.en: The Rav explains why Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur have no aliyah l'regel yet have bowing as in the Mikdash: the Mikdash comes to every Jew through time. He finds this in the custom of the chazzan beginning Hamelech from his place, and proves from pigul and from the creation that time is above place, so no enemy could destroy the Mikdash of time.

title.en: The sweet tefillos of Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Rav brings a hint from the Imrei Noam that Rosh Hashanah equals Beis HaMikdash in gematria, so a Jew should know he stands in the Mikdash and pray for Hashem's kingship over all. The challah dipped in honey hints that the tefillos of Rosh Hashanah are sweet, asking almost nothing for oneself.

title.en: Moshe's prayer and the holiness of Eretz Yisroel

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash on Moshe's words 'heaven and the heaven of heavens and the earth' and asks about their order and why Moshe instituted a prayer before prayer only at the end of forty years. With the Chasam Sofer he answers that only on entering Eretz Yisroel did Moshe feel a holiness greater than heaven, and with the Rambam-Ramban dispute he explains why the forty Aseres Yemei Teshuvah in the desert did not bring it earlier.

title.en: Adam's sin: life as freshness

summary.en: Returning to why bikkurim must be brought to the Mikdash, the Rav notes that Adam was created and sinned on Rosh Hashanah, bringing death into the world. Life means freshness and death means aging, so on Rosh Hashanah a Jew must repair this and serve Hashem with renewal.

title.en: The Mikdash, where nothing grows old

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Mikdash is the place of reishis where old age does not rule: the lechem hapanim stayed fresh, David never slept, Yaakov would not have slept in such a place, and a Levi who slept on watch was punished. Rosh Hashanah is the same, so one does not sleep then and asks not to be cast off to old age but to keep freshness all year.

title.en: The Slonimer Rebbe and the million dollars

summary.en: The Rav tells of the Beis Avraham of Slonim, whose young wife complained that he danced for an hour on Friday night, and the elder chassid who asked what she would do if he won a million dollars. He compares the crowd at a ballgame and says one should daven and learn with that freshness, as if each Shabbos were the first and last.

title.en: Souls in fruit and the first fig

summary.en: The Rav brings that souls enter fruit and are elevated when a Jew eats with a brachah, and explains that the fig which ripened first holds a soul of zrizus that belongs to the Mikdash, the place of reishis. Bikkurim are thus a tikkun for Adam's sin, and the fruit goes to the kohen, who eats it as the owner's emissary.

title.en: Zrizus and wishes for the new year

summary.en: The Rav sums up that the parsha of bikkurim urges zrizus and freshness, entering the point of reishis and carrying it through the year, which hastens the geulah of 'I will hasten it in its time'. He closes with wishes for the great shofar of geulah and a kesivah vachasimah tovah.

catalogTitle: באלול נעשה הקב"ה עיר מקלט של ישראל - ואין השטן יכול לנוס שמה (שייכות לפרשת שופטים)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains the Gemara that the Satan will mistakenly flee to Botzrah as a city of refuge, showing that a being in panic runs to its root, and that the month of Elul is a city of refuge where a Jew runs to Hashem and His Torah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Chasam Sofer on the mitzvah of appointing a king: a Jewish king draws down malchus shamayim, and the sin in Shmuel's time was asking for a king like the nations. Parshas Shoftim, read at the start of Elul, is a parsha of geulah, preparing for HaMelech HaKadosh on Rosh Hashanah. The three extra cities of refuge, never yet fulfilled, are the Rambam's proof from the Torah that Moshiach will come. He then explains the Gemara that the Satan will make three errors in fleeing to Botzrah, and answers them: a murderer has no place, every being in danger runs to its root like the sea dog to dry land, and the Satan's flight to Botzrah, the root of Edom, reveals that he is a deliberate sinner. Elul itself is a city of refuge; one runs there through Torah, a chavrusa, a hundred brachos said with kavanah and daily mussar, remembering one's name and mission on Rosh Hashanah.

en: According to the Chasam Sofer, a Jewish king's role is to draw malchus shamayim onto Klal Yisrael, unlike the kings of the nations who run their politics and wars.
The mitzvah of the three additional cities of refuge has never been fulfilled, so the Rambam brings it as a proof from the Torah that Moshiach will come and complete all 613 mitzvos.
A being in sudden danger acts on instinct and runs to its root, as the sea dog runs to dry land; the Satan's flight to Botzrah, the heart of Edom, reveals where he belongs.
A Jew's deliberate sin is at root unintentional because of the hidden love in his heart, while a gentile's unintentional sin is at root deliberate.
The whole month of Elul is a city of refuge, and the easiest way to run to Hashem in it is to run to the Torah.
Every person's name holds his mission, and Rosh Hashanah, the day of remembrance, demands that a Jew remember the mission he was sent into the world for.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer on the mitzvah of a king

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer that a Jewish king draws malchus shamayim onto Klal Yisrael, while the nations' kings run politics and wars; the sin in Shmuel's time was asking for a king like the nations instead of waiting for a king from Yehudah. He adds the Zohar that even Moshe needed Chur of Yehudah, and the Chasam Sofer's acronym of Mishkan.

title.en: Parshas Shoftim, a parsha of geulah for Elul

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shoftim, the first parsha read in Elul, is a parsha of geulah, since Elul is the month of Gad from whom Eliyahu comes, and it holds the king, navi and kohen. Accepting malchus shamayim prepares for saying HaMelech HaKadosh, and he brings the Heichal HaBrachah that had they waited for a king from Yehudah, Moshiach would have come then.

title.en: The unfulfilled mitzvah of three more cities

summary.en: The Rav brings the mitzvah in the parsha to add three more cities of refuge, which the Rambam cites as proof that Moshiach will come since it was never fulfilled. All 613 mitzvos were kept in the time of the Mikdash except this one, and the world waits for Moshiach to complete them.

title.en: The Satan's three errors about Botzrah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Makkos that the Satan will flee to Botzrah and make three errors: Botzrah is not Betzer, a refuge city protects only the unintentional killer, and only a man, not an angel. He asks how a great scholar errs where a child would not, why three errors are needed, and explains that an angel, a pure intellect, cannot err.

title.en: Can the Satan err, and why no teshuvah?

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yerushalmi, cited by Tosafos in Rosh Hashanah, that the Satan is confused by the shofar, and the Divrei Yoel that he is fooled measure for measure. If so he is unintentional, and the Rav asks further why his teshuvah should not help, since only a human court cannot see into the heart.

title.en: A murderer has no place

summary.en: The Rav brings the Sfas Emes in the name of the Chiddushei HaRim that a murderer has no place, and Hashem in His kindness gives the unintentional killer a place in the city of refuge. Every creation has a mission and therefore a place; the killer emptied a place, so he loses his own, like Kayin who became a wanderer, and like Klal Yisrael in galus.

title.en: Yerushalayim and the inner point of a Jew

summary.en: The Rav brings the Heichal HaBrachah that all the cities of refuge are included in Tzion and Yerushalayim, matching the words of Shema. The Kodesh HaKodashim, where no blemish reaches, corresponds to the inner point in every Jew's heart, the hidden love of the Tanya, so Yerushalayim, above place, gives a place to one who lost his.

title.en: Fleeing to one's root: the sea dog and Botzrah

summary.en: The Rav brings Reb Tzadok HaKohen on the Mishnah of the sea dog, which flees to dry land and so shows it belongs there; a Jew who runs to Torah in distress shows his root is there. He then discusses Botzrah, from Moav according to Rashi yet king-maker of Edom, and explains that it broke away to Edom because it belonged there, as the heart of Edom's harsh judgment and sword.

title.en: Why the Satan runs to Botzrah: the answer

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam on a forced get and the Yismach Moshe that a Jew's deliberate sin is unintentional while a gentile's unintentional sin is deliberate. Confused by Moshiach's shofar, the Satan runs on instinct to his root, Botzrah, the feminine side of the sitra achra according to the Ohr HaChaim, and not to Betzer; this reveals him as deliberate, so none of his three claims is an error, and teshuvah cannot help him.

title.en: Elul is a city of refuge: run to the Torah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that Rosh Hashanah is a city of refuge for every Jew and the Arizal that the whole of Elul is one, hinted in its acronym, with a wide road open in the days of mercy. Since words of Torah give refuge, the easiest way to run to Hashem in Elul is through Torah, and he advises a fixed chavrusa.

title.en: Moshiach and the last mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav compares Moshiach's bond with the mitzvah of cities of refuge to the Ropshitzer's bond with sukkah. This last unfulfilled mitzvah is held back by the Satan, and when a Jew runs to Hashem through Torah he awakens it, and the mitzvah itself cries out to be fulfilled, as mitzvos plead with a Jew to do them.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah: remembering one's name and mission

summary.en: The Rav explains Rosh Hashanah as the day of remembrance: Amalek makes one forget and the shofar awakens. Every creation has a mission held in its name, as Rashi explains the angel's words to Yaakov; Adam received his name and mission on Rosh Hashanah, and a rasha forgets his name because he forgot why he came, as when money becomes the goal rather than the means.

title.en: Whose messenger are you?

summary.en: The Rav describes stopping a Jew rushing through the street and asking whose messenger he is, and explains that the Satan's angel, who told Yaakov 'why do you ask my name', was created to make people forget their names. Rosh Hashanah demands that each Jew remember his mission.

title.en: Two counsels: a hundred brachos and mussar

summary.en: The Rav gives two counsels for remembering Hashem: the Rambam's hundred daily brachos, set against the forgetfulness linked to the Satan, said with kavanah, with bentching and even a short bracha from a siddur; and learning some mussar every day, as the Mishnah Berurah writes.

title.en: Avraham at the gate and the days of mercy

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that Avraham sits at the entrance of Gehinom, and closes that these forty days are days of great mercy and will, a wide road to run to Hashem, to Torah, mussar, the siddur and Tehillim, with a brachah for complete teshuvah and a good inscription.

catalogTitle: Every איד has the קדושה of one of the ימים טובים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that every Jew is a Shabbos, a letter of the Torah and one of the Yamim Tovim of Parshas Emor, and that the lechem hapanim, which stayed warm and fresh, shows that Hashem's love for even the lowest Jew never grows stale.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the idea that there are 600,000 Shabbosos, as there are 600,000 souls and 600,000 letters in the Torah, and each Jew has his own Shabbos. Parshas Emor adds that every Jew is also a moed: a talmid chacham who does not work is Shabbos, one who works only for his needs is Yom Tov, others are Chol Hamoed or Rosh Chodesh. Tisha B'Av is the one moed missing from the parsha: a Jew with great potential who went sour. He then turns to the lechem hapanim, which stayed fresh for nine days, and to the ben ish Mitzri, reconciling Rashi's two explanations: the camp was arranged like a Sefer Torah, the twelve challos stand for the tribes, and the mocker denied that Hashem's love for the lowly tribe of Dan stays warm. He links this to Haman's claim and to Purim, and closes with the week of Hod, Pesach Sheni and Lag BaOmer, which lift up the low Jew.

en: There are 600,000 Shabbosos corresponding to 600,000 souls and 600,000 letters of the Torah, and every Jew has his own Shabbos.
Every Jew is also a moed: according to his level he is Shabbos, Yom Tov, Chol Hamoed or Rosh Chodesh.
Tisha B'Av is a moed that went sour, like a Jew with great potential who went astray; with Mashiach it will become a great Yom Tov.
The camp in the desert was arranged like a Sefer Torah, each Jew a letter, so an outsider in the camp of Dan would be like an extra letter.
The freshness of the lechem hapanim shows that Hashem's love for every Jew, even the tribe of Dan, stays warm and fresh, and the ben ish Mitzri denied this.
Haman made the same claim, that Hashem's love for the Jews had grown old, so the parsha of the ben ish Mitzri belongs with Purim.
The week of Hod, with Pesach Sheni and Lag BaOmer, like Purim, lifts up and encourages the low Jew.

title.en: Every Jew has his own Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav says no two Shabbosos are alike: there are 600,000 Shabbosos, one for every soul, as there are 600,000 letters in the Torah. He shows how one letter is made of several, so only Hashem can count them.

title.en: Every Jew is a moed; the talmid chacham as Shabbos

summary.en: From 'eileh moadei Hashem' the Rav learns that every Jew is a moed. Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai is Shabbos; melacha comes from the 39 curses of the sin, so Shabbos and the talmid chacham are free of it, while the weekdays, like ordinary people, provide for Shabbos.

title.en: Yom Tov, Chol Hamoed and Rosh Chodesh Jews

summary.en: The Rav describes the talmid chacham who works only for his daily needs as Yom Tov, one who works a bit more as Chol Hamoed, and women, who have more emunah, as Rosh Chodesh. Every moed is according to its level.

title.en: Tisha B'Av, the moed that went sour

summary.en: The Rav asks which moed is missing from Emor and answers Tisha B'Av, which is called a moed. It is like a boy with all the makings of a talmid chacham who went astray; with Mashiach it will become a great Yom Tov.

title.en: The lechem hapanim and the ben ish Mitzri

summary.en: The Rav describes the lechem hapanim, which stayed warm and fresh nine days, and then the ben ish Mitzri. He brings Rashi's two explanations of 'vayeitzei': he mocked the lechem hapanim, or he left Moshe Rabbeinu's beis din after being refused a place in the camp of Dan, and then cursed.

title.en: The camp arranged as a Sefer Torah

summary.en: The Rav asks why the neighbors objected when the desert had room for all. He answers that the camps were arranged by prophecy like a Sefer Torah, each Jew a letter, and an extra letter invalidates it. He adds that two opposing explanations can be one, and so are Rashi's two.

title.en: Twelve challos and the tribe of Dan

summary.en: The Rav reconstructs the argument: the twelve challos correspond to the tribes and hold secrets of all Klal Yisrael, which the Arizal, in his zemer, says are too deep even for him. Dan was the last camp and many of Dan were outside the clouds, so the man claimed Dan did not matter.

title.en: Each challah separate, each challah fresh

summary.en: The Rav explains that each challah is baked on its own, showing that even Dan has its own importance, and that the challos staying fresh shows Hashem's love for every Jew stays warm. Dan was joined with Yehudah in building the Mishkan. The mocker denied this love, so Rashi's two explanations are one.

title.en: The Arizal on who the ben ish Mitzri was

summary.en: The Rav brings the Arizal that the ben ish Mitzri returned as a gilgul more than a thousand years later as the founder of Christianity, who taught that Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael had cooled and the nations had replaced them.

title.en: Haman and the lechem hapanim: Purim

summary.en: The Rav explains why the lechem hapanim hints at Purim: the Gemara reads the names of Achashverosh's advisors as the korbanos and the lechem hapanim, and Haman's 'yeshno' means the love has grown old. Haman made the same claim as the ben ish Mitzri.

title.en: The week of Hod lifts the low Jew

summary.en: The Rav matches the Yamim Tovim to the middos and says Purim is Hod. In the week of Hod, Pesach Sheni and Lag BaOmer give a place to the low Jew; Purim and Lag BaOmer fall on the same weekday. He concludes that the love for Jews remains warm and fresh forever.

catalogTitle: דרוש בענין - זמני תשובה הנרמזים בפרשיות התורה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the forgotten and lost souls of the end of days are bound to the very beginning, that Hashem never forgets them though Amalek wants them lost, and that Elul is the time of returning the lost, to be served with the fire that separates Yisrael from Amalek.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Chasam Sofer on parshas Ki Savo, which links Amalek, 'the first of the nations', to bikkurim and to the last fruits. Yisrael are Hashem's first produce, and bikkurim, the earliest fruits, belong in Yerushalayim, the first place created. Opposite them stand the forgotten fruits, shikchah, leket and pe'ah, which the Rav compares to the neglected souls of the last generation; yet these are tied to the beginning, as seen with Rus and with the evyon who is Moshiach. He then asks why Haman's silver ignored the 1,775 shekels that became the hooks of the Mishkan, and why Moshe forgot them: they were souls of shikchah, outside the curtain, and Hashem reminded him. Dan, the tribe that returned lost things, and Esther stand against Amalek, who wants Jews lost. Elul is the time of returning the lost. Finally, Haman's money was cold, while Jewish giving carries fire; the Rav urges davening and learning with fire.

en: Bikkurim, the earliest-ripening fruits, are brought to Yerushalayim because they belong to the place that was created first, the Even Shesiyah from which the world was founded.
The forgotten fruits, shikchah, leket and pe'ah, correspond to the neglected souls of the last generation before Moshiach, yet these are bound to the beginning and hold a spark of Moshiach.

The 1,775 shekels that became the hooks outside the Mishkan's curtain came from Jews whose half-shekel did not enter the sockets; they are souls of shikchah, which is why Moshe forgot them and Hashem reminded him.
Amalek wants Jews lost and forgotten, while Dan, who gathered and returned what was lost, and Esther, whose name hints at avedah, are the counterforce of hashavas aveidah.
Elul, like Adar, stands at the end of a half-year and is the time of hashavas aveidah, when the forgotten souls are gathered back.
The difference between Yisrael and Amalek is esh, fire: Haman gave cold money, while Jewish giving, davening and learning must carry fire.

machatzis hashekel and the hooks of the Mishkan

title.en: The Chasam Sofer's reading and the bikkurim

summary.en: The Rav quotes the Chasam Sofer on Ki Savo, linking Amalek as 'first of the nations', bikkurim and the last fruits, and says it needs explaining. He describes Yisrael as Hashem's first produce and explains that bikkurim, the fruits that ripen first, are brought to Yerushalayim, the place created first.

title.en: The forgotten fruits and the souls of the end

summary.en: The Rav compares shikchah, pe'ah and leket to the forgotten souls of the last generation, and shows they are tied to the beginning: the end of the Torah links to Bereishis, Rus gathered shikchah and became the root of Beis David, and the Ohr HaChaim reads the evyon as Moshiach.

title.en: Shavuos, leket and shikchah

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Torah inserts leket and pe'ah into the passage of the shtei halechem on Shavuos, and answers that the neglected souls belong to the festival of first fruits as well. He adds that one may never belittle a simple Jew, and shows how shikchah in Ki Seitzei is also tied to reishis.

title.en: Haman's shekels and the forgotten 1,775

summary.en: Turning to zechiras Amalek, the Rav brings the Gemara that the Jews' shekalim preceded Haman's, and Tosafos that Haman's silver was set against the half-shekel. He asks why Haman paid nothing for the 1,775 shekels that became the hooks, and how Moshe, who never forgot, forgot what he did with them.

title.en: The stragglers of Dan and Hashem's love

summary.en: The Rav brings the Targum Yonasan that the nechshalim Amalek attacked were men of Dan who carried idols and were cast out of the clouds of glory. He describes Hashem's anger at Amalek for attacking even them, Hashem's love for every Jew, and explains that Amalek thought forgotten Jews do not matter, but Hashem does not forget them.

title.en: Dan the restorer, Amalek the destroyer

summary.en: The Rav explains that Dan, at the end of the camp and prone to idolatry, was a forgotten tribe and was given the mitzvah of returning lost things. Amalek is the opposite, the one who makes Jews lost, as seen in Haman's decree; Dan's name, 'danani Elokim', shows that the lost one will be found again.

title.en: The hooks outside the curtain

summary.en: The Rav answers his questions: the half-shekel of the 3,550 extra Jews did not become sockets but the silver hooks, the only part of the Mishkan outside its curtain. These are souls of shikchah, so Moshe forgot them, and Hashem, who never forgets, reminded him; Haman likewise thought he need not pay for forgotten Jews.

title.en: Esther, the soul of the lost who are sought

summary.en: The Rav explains that the great shofar of Elul and Tishrei awakens the lost Jews, and that Esther, who stood against Haman's plan to destroy, is the soul of hashavas aveidah. She is the hiding at the end of exile, a lost one who is sought, 'ka'asher avadti avadti', and her name hints at avedah.

title.en: Elul and Adar: the time of returning the lost

summary.en: Bringing the Arizal that the months divide into two halves, the Rav shows that Elul and Adar both close a half-year and are times of hashavas aveidah. He links this to L'Dovid Hashem ori, to Chag ha'Asif, and to the Arizal's reading of Elul as matanos la'evyonim, the giving of tzedakah to the lowly in whom Moshiach is found.

title.en: Back to the Chasam Sofer; the cry of Elul

summary.en: The Rav returns to the Chasam Sofer: not only the first fruits but the last ones must be sanctified, unlike Amalek who held the forgotten need no redemption. He then explains that in Elul a Jew must cry out to Hashem that he is lost at the end of time, like Dovid's 'ta'isi kaseh oved', and Hashem will help.

title.en: Parashas hakesef and the fire in the Mikdash

summary.en: The Rav brings the Divrei Shmuel and Rashi on 'parashas hakesef' and asks what explanation silver needs. He explains from 'tocho ratzuf ahavah' that the heart of the Mikdash was not its silver and gold but the burning love of Jewish hearts, which is what Hashem showed Moshe with the coin of fire.

title.en: Kesef with its filling: the fire of Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav explains that Haman gave cold money with an evil intent, while the spelled-out letters of kesef equal esh, as in the 'kesef malei' of Avraham and Dovid. Yisrael minus Amalek is also esh: Yisrael gives with fire and Amalek cools. He brings the tochachah's 'besimchah', and the Shaarei Teshuvah and Yeshayahu against mitzvos done by rote.

title.en: Davening with fire; the Jew in Stolin

summary.en: The Rav describes the cold, habitual davening of exile and calls for fresh, fiery davening and learning, connecting 'desheinim vera'ananim' to Rosh Hashanah and stressing the worth of Aleinu. He tells of a Jew in the Stolin shtibel in Williamsburg who rejoiced that he was let in, and applies 'berov chasdecha avo veisecha' to every entry into shul.

title.en: Every day a Rosh Hashanah; encouraging Jews

summary.en: The Rav applies 'achas sha'alti' and Rashi's 'every day as new' to approaching each day with freshness, as in Eretz Yisrael every day is like Rosh Hashanah. He says Jews today must be encouraged with Hashem's love, as Malachi did, not rebuked, and closes with Elul, the coming Shemitah year and a tefillah for the great shofar.

catalogTitle: חודש הששי כנגד יוסף וקדושת היסוד; ששי מכין לשביעי

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Elul, the sixth month, belongs to Yosef HaTzaddik, who was raised from the twelve tribes to the seven shepherds, and that like erev Shabbos it prepares for Tishrei, the month of David.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Chasam Sofer on Shoftim: each tribe has its own path, judges and even halachos, while the Avos and Yerushalayim, where 'the tribes went up', stand above that division, at the level of the fiftieth gate. He then asks why Yaakov loved Yosef as his 'ben zekunim' if he taught him only five orders of Mishnah. Building on the seven shepherds (Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov, Moshe, Aharon, Yosef, David) who correspond to the seven days and to the orders of Mishnah, he explains that Yosef, Friday and Taharos, mastered his order himself, and that this is how Yaakov sensed from the grain of Egypt that Yosef lived. Elul is Yosef's month and his mikdash in Shiloh, open without walls like a king in the field, preparing for Tishrei as erev Shabbos prepares for Shabbos. He closes with guarding the eyes, teshuvah, tzedakah and the trembling of the Elul shofar.

en: Each tribe has its own root, path and judges, but the Avos and Yerushalayim stand above the division of the tribes; there 'the tribes went up' to a level beyond comprehension.

The seven shepherds (Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov, Moshe, Aharon, Yosef, David) influence all of Klal Yisrael, and Yosef was raised from the tribes to be one of them, with Ephraim and Menashe taking his place among the tribes.
The seven days of the week correspond to the seven shepherds and to the orders of Mishnah; Yosef is Friday and the order of Taharos, which he mastered himself.
Elul, the sixth month, belongs to Yosef according to the seven shepherds, and Tishrei to David; Elul prepares for Tishrei as erev Shabbos prepares for Shabbos.
Yosef's mikdash in Shiloh had no wall, so its kodashim could be eaten wherever it was seen; so too in Elul the King is in the field and anyone can approach Him.
Yosef's midah is yesod and tzedakah, which draws down chesed beyond what is earned, and Elul is the time of teshuvah, tefillah and tzedakah.
