Beis Lechem and Malchus Beis David

title.en: Yovel, Shavuos and the eighth week

summary.en: The Rav compares the count of Shemitah and Yovel to the count of Sefirah: the fiftieth day is also the first of an eighth week, above the seven days of nature. Yovel means returning to the roots, when the servant goes back to his family and fields to their owners, and on Shavuos a Jew returns to Hashem.

title.en: Sold to an idol, and why 'eiker' only here

summary.en: The Rav reads the passuk of a Jew sold to a gentile and to 'eiker', which Rashi explains as serving an idol as its attendant, a very great fall. He brings a midrash that it is called 'eiker' because it will be uprooted, and asks why the Torah first says so here, connecting it to Shavuos, when the heavens come down to earth.

title.en: Why he fell, and how Yovel brings him back

summary.en: The Rav explains from the Gemara that the man was sold because he traded in Shemitah produce, until he lost his kedushas Yisrael. Having violated Shemitah he cannot feel the holiness of Shabbos and does not want Shemitah to free him, but the point in every Jew that is never lost flares up at Yovel and brings him back to the mishpacha of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Hashem protests: the idol will be uprooted

summary.en: The Rav explains that when a Jew sinks so low that he tolerates serving an idol, Hashem grows angry at the avodah zarah for swallowing His child and declares it will be uprooted. He links this to the bracha against heretics added to Shemoneh Esrei in the days of Rabban Gamliel, which also speaks of uprooting.

title.en: Nineteen 'geulos' and the brachos of Shemoneh Esrei

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al HaTurim that the root 'geulah' appears nineteen times in the sedra, matching the nineteen brachos of Shemoneh Esrei. Counting them, he finds that the redemption of the man sold to the idol is the twelfth, the one who redeems him is the thirteenth, the tzaddikim, and the next ones correspond to Yerushalayim and to Malchus Beis David, so the sedra itself is a tefillah for the geulah.

title.en: End of Sefirah, and Rus's Jewish soul

summary.en: The Rav explains that Sefirah divides into thirds and is practically finished, so the remaining weeks are preparation for Shavuos, the day of Yovel. On Shavuos we read Rus, and he brings from the Chida and the Alshich that a convert has a Jewish soul from the start, which is why Rus is said to 'return' from Moav; a Jewish soul born among the nations has no rest until it comes back to its root.

title.en: A diamond in the garbage; Yovel in Beis Lechem

summary.en: The Rav explains that the soul of Malchus Beis David was hidden in Rus, in the house of Eglon king of Moav, so that the Satan would not suspect it, like a diamond hidden in a garbage can. He then brings from the sefarim that Eretz Yisrael is a Sefer Torah, and suggests on his own that the parsha of Yovel is written in Beis Lechem Yehudah, which is why Rus returned there.

title.en: Rachel, the mother buried on the road

summary.en: The Rav brings the Maharal that Rachel, the akeres habayis, is the mother and root of all Klal Yisrael. She was buried on the road to Beis Lechem, the place of Yovel and Malchus, so that when the Jews went into galus she would weep, and Hashem answered her with the promise that the children will return.

title.en: The monkey's imitation and the shaking out

summary.en: The Rav brings that the sitra achra imitates kedushah like a monkey imitates a person. The Rambam's sign of the true Mashiach is gathering in the dispersed of Israel, a Yovel; the nations, sensing that Beis Lechem is the place of Yovel, invented their own messiah born there. In the end Hashem will shake all impurity out of Eretz Yisrael, and at Kever Rachel one can feel Rachel's weeping and Hashem's promise that the children will return.

title.en: The Rashbam, and Shavuos as a wedding

summary.en: The Rav explains that the sedra is the fabric of its Shabbos, so this Shabbos is a Shemoneh Esrei. Yovel was hinted in Mishpatim, where the Rashbam reads 'forever' literally; the Rav explains it as what the servant deserves, while Yovel still rescues him. Shavuos is a teshuvah of return and a wedding of Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and he closes that the remaining weeks are for polishing the middos in preparation.

catalogTitle: צד א: ביאור קריאת העקידה דיום ב' דר"ה וההפטרה "מרחוק ה' נראה לי ואהבת עולם אהבתיך"

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that at the Akeidah, when Avraham saw Hashem only 'from afar', he went through the trial of the last generation before Moshiach and planted in his children the power to hold on to simple emunah in a time of hester panim, which is the message of the second day of Rosh Hashanah and its haftarah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the mitzvah of appointing a king and the Rambam's teaching that the Torah speaks of Moshiach in three places, which match the signs of Moshiach. Appointing a king is fulfilled by bringing Moshiach, by attaching oneself to a tzaddik, and above all by accepting Hashem's kingship with Krias Shema, the mitzvah of Rosh Hashanah, said with closed eyes in simple emunah. He then turns to the Akeidah, Avraham's tenth and greatest trial: Avraham fell from his level, saw Hashem only 'from afar', faced unanswerable questions about the promise of Yitzchak, and still went without questioning. Following the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, the Rav explains that the last trial of Klal Yisrael before Moshiach is hester panim, and Avraham's emunah gives the 'heel' generation its strength. He ends with the haftarah 'from afar Hashem appeared to me... with eternal love I loved you', Esther's self-sacrifice, and the task of the chevra to spread emunah.

en: The Rav brings the Rambam that the Torah speaks of Moshiach in three parshiyos, Balak, Shoftim and Nitzavim, which match the signs by which Moshiach is recognized.
The mitzvah of appointing a king is fulfilled by accepting Hashem's kingship, and above all through Krias Shema, the mitzvah of Rosh Hashanah.
Shema is said with closed eyes because the emunah it accepts is simple faith, not knowledge or investigation.
At the Akeidah Avraham saw Hashem only 'from afar': he lost his clear closeness and faced unanswerable questions, yet went without questioning.
Since the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, Klal Yisrael's last trial before Moshiach is that of 'from afar', a test of emunah in hester panim.
The haftarah teaches that even when Hashem is seen only from afar, His eternal love for the Jewish people has not ceased.
The Rav says the particular task of the chevra is to believe so strongly that they draw emunah onto all of Klal Yisrael.

candidateTopics: Krias Shema and kabbalas ol malchus shamayim
haftarah of the second day of Rosh Hashanah

title.en: Appointing a king and Moshiach in the Torah

summary.en: After brief opening words about the importance of emunah today, the Rav turns to the mitzvah of appointing a king in this week's parsha and brings the Rambam that belief in Moshiach comes from the Torah itself, which mentions him in three places: Balak, the added cities of refuge in Shoftim, and Nitzavim.

title.en: The three signs of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam's signs of Moshiach: he fights the wars of Hashem, strengthens the keeping of the Torah, and builds the Beis HaMikdash and gathers the exiles, and matches each to one of the three parshiyos; he adds that adding three cities of refuge is the one mitzvah never yet fulfilled.

title.en: Crowning Hashem: Moshiach, the tzaddik and emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains that 'appoint a king' is fulfilled by bringing Moshiach through Torah, chesed and tefillah, by accepting a tzaddik through whom one comes close to Hashem, and in Elul by accepting Hashem's kingship through Krias Shema. Everything rests on emunah, and a chevra that works on emunah draws emunah onto the whole world, just as a heretic draws heresy.

title.en: Shema: the mitzvah of Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Rav calls the Akeidah, read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, the foundation of emunah. Every day has its own mitzvah, and he suggests that the mitzvah of Rosh Hashanah is Shema Yisrael, the tenth pasuk of Malchiyos; it is said with closed eyes because it is simple emunah, not knowledge.

title.en: The tenth trial: seeing Hashem from afar

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Akeidah, the tenth trial, is greater than the first trial in Ur Kasdim. With the Zohar he explains that Avraham could have asked how Hashem's promise of offspring through Yitzchak would be kept, yet chose not to question and went with closed eyes; 'he saw the place from afar' means he saw Hashem from a distance, and all his hopes for the Jewish people seemed about to be shattered.

title.en: Offspring only through the Akeidah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ohr HaChaim that Yitzchak by nature could not have children, and only through the Akeidah, when his soul returned, could the promise of offspring be fulfilled; right after it Rivkah's birth is announced. The simple answer, that Hashem never said to slaughter Yitzchak, did not occur to Avraham, and that was the trial: he lost his clear perception and saw Hashem from afar.

title.en: The last trial of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: With the Ramban's rule that the deeds of the fathers are a sign for the children, the Rav explains that Klal Yisrael too must pass ten trials through the generations, and the last, before Moshiach, is the trial of 'from afar': hester panim, when tzaddikim are not permitted to show wonders and many fall into doubts. Because Avraham held on to emunah, there will always be Jews and tzaddikim who hold on to it.

title.en: Avraham's emunah reaches the heel

summary.en: The Rav explains that at the Akeidah Avraham was thrown down to the state of the generation of ikvesa d'Meshicha, with all its winds of heresy, and planted emunah in it. Bringing Chavakuk 'the tzaddik lives by his emunah', the shiur komah of the generations from head to heel (Pri Tzaddik), and 'eikev asher shamata bekoli', he concludes that Avraham's emunah reached down to the heel, the last generation.

title.en: Shema's hidden word: emes

summary.en: The Rav brings the Shulchan Aruch that the 248 words of Shema correspond to the 248 limbs; since three are missing, the shliach tzibbur repeats them, ending with 'emes'. Shema is the head and 'emes' the heel, and in ikvesa d'Meshicha the truth is hidden, as the Gemara says; the leader cries out 'emes' and the whole congregation with him, as Malachi says of those who fear Hashem.

title.en: Rosh Hashanah night, the shofar and the second day

summary.en: The Rav compares Yitzchak's soul departing and returning at the Akeidah to Rosh Hashanah night, when the old year departs and the new life comes only with the tekios. Avraham's holding on to Hashem's kingship earned the loving call 'Avraham, Avraham' and the shofar of Yitzchak's ram, which disperses the clouds; the second day of Rosh Hashanah, with its Akeidah and haftarah, awakens the merit of Jews who hold on to emunah.

title.en: 'With eternal love' and Esther's self-sacrifice

summary.en: The Rav explains the haftarah: in hester panim a Jew might think Hashem has abandoned him, but the navi says that although Hashem is seen from afar, He loves with eternal love. He connects this to Esther, hinted in 'haster astir', who sacrificed even her good name by inviting Haman, the same quality as Avraham's, and to the double, loving call 'Avraham, Avraham'.

title.en: Waiting for the great shofar

summary.en: The Rav describes the present as the night of Rosh Hashanah of history, before the shofar of Moshiach disperses the clouds, the last of the trials, when one must strengthen oneself against those who try to take away emunah. He gives the chevra its task, to draw emunah onto all of Klal Yisrael, and ends with blessings for the shofar of redemption and a good inscription.

catalogTitle: צד ב: תורה מאדמו"ר מסאטמאר זצ”ל

oneLiner.en: The Rav relates a Rosh Hashanah derashah of the Satmar Rebbe: Hashem should have mercy on Klal Yisrael by a kal vachomer from Eisav's tears, the shofar of a ram completes the akeidah by joining thought to deed, and in a year without shofar Shabbos itself must plead for us.

abstract.en: The Rav relates, largely in the Satmar Rebbe's own words, a derashah said before tekios on Rosh Hashanah. If Eisav earned his blessings through three tears, Hashem must surely have mercy on the Jewish people, who have poured out rivers of tears; this is the 'mishpat' of the G-d of Yaakov. The Gemara's shofar of a ram is explained through Reb Zusha's teaching that Hashem joins one person's longing to another's deed: the ram completed the akeidah in deed, Avraham's longing joined the circumcision of his household, and Moshe was told 'rav lach' because his longing sufficed. The derashah then laments the bitter years of exile, reads 'im yitaka shofar' as amazement that no one trembles while the great shofar is still not blown, and explains that when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbos, Shabbos is the advocate, so one must reconcile with it and keep it properly. Shabbos, Tishrei and the shemitah year are three releases from debts, and the talk closes on tefillah in Eretz Yisrael and in exile.

en: If Eisav merited all his blessings through three tears, then by kal vachomer Hashem must have mercy on Jews who have poured out rivers of tears.
Following Reb Zusha, Hashem combines the longing of one who cannot act with the deed of one whose intent is lacking, so the mitzvah becomes complete.
The ram completed the akeidah in deed, which is why the shofar of a ram recalls the akeidah itself.
The navi's amazement in 'im yitaka shofar' is that people do not tremble while the great shofar is still not blown and they remain in exile.
When there is no shofar because Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbos, Shabbos is the advocate, so one must reconcile with Shabbos and keep it as it should be kept.
Shabbos, the seventh month and the shemitah year are each a release, and their meeting is a time to ask Hashem to erase all our debts.

title.en: A kal vachomer from Eisav's tears

summary.en: Joining the derashah in the middle, the Rav relates the Satmar Rebbe's kal vachomer: if Eisav earned his blessings with three tears, Hashem must have mercy on Jews who shed rivers of tears. The Rebbe then laments the broken hearts of the time and calls on everyone to take stock before tekios.

title.en: The ram completes the akeidah

summary.en: The derashah asks why the shofar is of a ram rather than recalling the akeidah of Yitzchak directly, and answers with Reb Zusha's teaching that Hashem joins one person's thought to another's deed. The Satmar Rebbe applies it to 'nimolu itto', to the ram at the akeidah, and to Moshe Rabbeinu's plea to enter Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: Our tekios joined to the tzaddikim's kavanos

summary.en: In earlier generations tzaddikim could have the kavanos of the tekios; today one asks Hashem to join our deeds to their intentions so the mitzvah is complete. The derashah then raises the question of how the Satan is confused by the second blowing year after year; the answer is largely garbled.

title.en: Bitter years and 'im yitaka shofar'

summary.en: The Satmar Rebbe cries over the years that have passed without salvation and asks how long. He explains the passuk 'im yitaka shofar' as the navi's amazement that the great shofar has not yet been blown and people still do not tremble, and ends with a tefillah for a bright chasimah and the geulah.

title.en: Shabbos as the good friend before the King

summary.en: A mashal from sefarim: a man whose usual advocate cannot come must reconcile with another friend dear to the king. The shofar pleads for us every year; when Rosh Hashanah is on Shabbos, Shabbos pleads instead, so one must make peace with Shabbos and honor it with holiness, Torah and Shabbos speech, not only by refraining from melachah.

title.en: Three shemitos together

summary.en: The shemitah year, 'Shabbos laShem', is a whole year of Shabbos and a time of releasing debts. Every Shabbos, every seventh month and every seventh year is a shemitah, and when all three meet on Rosh Hashanah one asks Hashem to erase all our debts.

title.en: Yerushalayim, the house of tefillah

summary.en: Yerushalayim is the house of tefillah in place, as Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and Sukkos are in time, and Chevron is joined to it. On Rosh Hashanah Hashem's kingship reaches the whole world, so He sees the pitiful spiritual state of Jews in exile; the talk closes with mutual tefillah and wishes for a good year and the geulah.

catalogTitle: שבת זו מתקן כל השבתות שבשנה - וקראת לשבת עונג!

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches that Shabbos Shuva rectifies every Shabbos of the year and calls for preparing to feel the delight of Shabbos, then shows how the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah are reflected in the pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Arizal's teaching that each of the seven days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur rectifies its weekday for the whole year, so Shabbos Shuva rectifies every Shabbos. This year Rosh Hashanah and the first day of Sukkos fall on Shabbos, with no shofar and no lulav, so the Shabbos itself must plead and fight for us, and one must make peace with it. He then explains 'call the Shabbos a delight': coming to Shabbos with a clear head, learning on Shabbos, saying Shir Hashirim with its meaning, going to the mikveh and eating every bite in honor of Shabbos, with a mashal of a thirsty man who drank foul water before finding a sweet spring. In the second part he matches the 122 days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah to the 122 pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu, and explains the two orders of the ushpizin through the dispute about a chazakah and Moshe's three signs.

en: Each of the seven days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur rectifies that weekday for the whole year, so Shabbos Shuva rectifies all the Shabbosos.
When the shofar or the lulav is not taken because of Shabbos, the Shabbos itself pleads and fights for the Jews, provided they are at peace with it.
'Call the Shabbos a delight' requires preparation: a clear head, learning on Shabbos and learning the meaning of Shir Hashirim.
A soul sated with worldly pleasures cannot feel the true delight of Shabbos, like a thirsty man who drank foul water before reaching a sweet spring.
The work of the Yamim Noraim continues until Shemini Atzeres and even until the last day of Chanukah.
Hashem gave Moshe three signs so as not to decide between Rebbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on whether two or three times make a chazakah.
The 122 days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah correspond to the 122 pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu.

title.en: Shabbos Shuva rectifies every Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Arizal that each of the seven days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur rectifies the same weekday for the whole year, so this Shabbos rectifies all the year's Shabbosos. He asks what happens when Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbos and the shofar is not blown, and answers that the Shabbos itself pleads for the Jews if they are on good terms with it; so this year one must especially accept to keep Shabbos and make peace with it.

title.en: The Shabbos fights when there is no lulav

summary.en: The Rav describes the battle of the Yamim Noraim as continuing past Yom Kippur to Hoshana Rabbah, Shemini Atzeres and the last day of Chanukah, comparing the hakafos with the four species to the circling of Yericho. When the first day of Sukkos falls on Shabbos and no lulav is taken, the Shabbos fights for us; and since the esrog is like the heart, Hashem is the heart of Yisroel and Shabbos is His name, the Shabbos itself is our esrog, so Shabbos Shuva is the time to appease the Shabbos.

title.en: Making Shabbos a delight

summary.en: The Rav explains 'and you shall call the Shabbos a delight' and says one must come to Shabbos with a clear head, not exhausted; learning on Shabbos is worth far more than staying up Thursday night. He urges a fixed seder of learning on Shabbos and introduces the saying of Shir Hashirim before Shabbos, composed by Shlomo HaMelech in an era that was a foretaste of the days of Moshiach.

title.en: Saying Shir Hashirim with its meaning

summary.en: The Rav tells of R' Mordechai of Lechovitch, who was pleased with a simple chassid who said Shir Hashirim with fervor without knowing its meaning, and says that today one must learn the meaning of the words. He brings verses that express Hashem's love for Klal Yisroel as a chasan for a kallah, the Gemara that Shabbos is one sixtieth of Olam Haba, and 'I sleep but my heart is awake', and calls for accepting to say Shir Hashirim on erev Shabbos.

title.en: The thirsty man and the sweet spring

summary.en: From 'a people satiated with delight' in the Friday night tefillah the Rav says that a Jew who does not feel the delight of Shabbos must have himself repaired, by asking an ehrlicher talmid chacham. He cites 'many waters cannot extinguish the love' and tells a mashal of a thirsty traveller who quenched his thirst with foul water and later found a spring of sweet water he no longer wanted: the soul, which seeks delight, is sated by worldly pleasures and cannot feel the true delight of Shabbos.

title.en: Going to the mikveh before Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav speaks about preparing for Shabbos by going to the mikveh. He brings a Midrash about Avraham Avinu's tree and says that when someone came to enter under the wings of the Shechinah, Avraham spoke to him about emunah and also about mikveh; he mentions the Rambam regarding Ezra's time and the chinuch of children, and says Jews go to the mikveh on erev Shabbos because receiving Shabbos must begin with preparation.

title.en: Every bite in honor of Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav describes Shabbos as a union of Hashem and Klal Yisroel and says the purpose of the Shabbos meals is not a good time but that every bite be in honor of Shabbos. He tells of a poor Karliner chassid who said over his challah and his fish that they were for the honor of Shabbos, and explains that a mitzvah or a page of Gemara on Shabbos is worth far more than on a weekday, since Shabbos is a taste of Olam Haba.

title.en: The delight of the soul

summary.en: The Rav says that on Shabbos one should feel the delight of the soul, in davening and in attachment to Hashem, mentioning the holy R' Shlomo of Karlin, and that no minute of Shabbos should go to waste. He asks for time on Shabbos for learning the sedra with Rashi and commentaries, which brings a person closer to Hashem.

title.en: From the forty days to Zos Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that during the first forty days one may still daven about the forming child, and applies it to the forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur. Whoever has not completed his work can still add until Shemini Atzeres and even until the last day of Chanukah, and even the greatest tzaddik can still add as long as Moshiach has not come.

title.en: Haazinu and the two orders of the ushpizin

summary.en: The Rav says that the pesukim of Haazinu correspond to the days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Shemini Atzeres, so that each day's avodah can be found in its pasuk. He presents two orders of the ushpizin, the Arizal's with Moshe and Aharon before Yosef and another with Yosef after the Avos, and notes that the pasuk where Moshe's name first appears in Haazinu matches Moshe's day in the Arizal's order, so Yosef must also be hinted there.

title.en: Three signs and the dispute over chazakah

summary.en: The Rav asks why Hashem gave Moshe three signs when he said the people would not believe him. He brings the dispute of Rebbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel whether a chazakah is set by two or three times, and the Rambam that a navi is established by signs; since both views are the words of the living G-d and Torah law is decided by the sages of the generation, Hashem gave a third sign so as not to decide between them.

title.en: Both orders of the ushpizin are true

summary.en: The Rav applies the same idea to Haazinu: on the days where the two orders of the ushpizin differ, one figure is named explicitly and the other only hinted, Moshe explicitly with Yosef hinted, and Aharon explicitly with Yosef hinted, so that Hashem does not decide which order is primary. He connects Yosef to guarding the bris, and suggests that the same dispute appears in how the hadassim, aravos and lulav are arranged.

title.en: 122 days, 122 pesukim and the hidden light

summary.en: The Rav counts 122 days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to the last day of Chanukah and matches them to the 122 pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu, explaining why Vezos Habracha is not counted. On Zos Chanukah the hidden light of creation is revealed; one may look at it but not yet use it, as hinted in the last pasuk of Haazinu, 'from afar you will see the land'. He closes that the pesukim learned in this period are capsules that sustain the whole year.

catalogTitle: An Explanation of “מה ענין שמיטה אצל הר סיני”, & Proof from this פרשה of משיח

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Shemitah is tied to Har Sinai because, like the giving of the Torah, it is a public, witnessed break in the laws of nature that proves the Torah true, but one that lasts in every generation.

abstract.en: The Rav returns to Rashi's question of what Shemitah has to do with Har Sinai and says last week's answer does not fully explain why Shemitah was chosen. First he shows hints of Mashiach in Behar-Bechukosai: the Arizal's hope for Mashiach before Shavuos, Yaakov written with a vav, and the Ramak's teaching that the fiftieth mention of Yetzias Mitzrayim is in this sedra. He then reviews why Jewish emunah, unlike faiths founded by one man, rests on events seen by multitudes: Yetzias Mitzrayim, the mann, and above all Matan Torah, where every Jew heard Hashem. The survival of Klal Yisrael and of Torah, and the Torah's daring promises, still testify. Shemitah is such a promise: the stories of Komemiyus and the rains of the sixth year show nature bending. So Shemitah is a lasting Har Sinai, and the Rav closes with Yovel, the return, and a brachah to bring Mashiach.

en: Saying that every detail of every mitzvah was given at Sinai does not explain why the Torah chose Shemitah to teach it.
Jewish emunah, unlike faiths founded on one man's word, rests on events witnessed by millions, which no one can deny.
Matan Torah, where every Jew became a navi and heard Hashem, is the root of emunah and of belief in Moshe Rabbeinu's prophecy.
The Torah makes promises that only its Giver could make, such as the safety of the land during the pilgrimages and the blessing of the sixth year.
Shemitah is tied to Har Sinai because, like Matan Torah, it openly defies the laws of nature, but unlike Sinai it lasts forever.

title.en: Why Shemitah of all mitzvos?

summary.en: The Rav recalls Rashi's question of what Shemitah has to do with Har Sinai and asks why the Torah did not use another mitzvah, such as milah or meat and milk. He reviews last week's answer linking Sinai, the fiftieth day, to Yovel and the shofar, and says he will approach it from a different angle. He then brings the Arizal's hope that Mashiach would come before Shavuos.

title.en: Hints of Mashiach in this sedra

summary.en: Continuing the theme of Mashiach before Shavuos, the Rav brings Yaakov written with a vav in this sedra as a pledge for Eliyahu to herald Mashiach, and the Ramak's teaching that the fiftieth mention of Yetzias Mitzrayim, which stands for Mashiach, is at the end of the tochachah. He adds that the 49 curses are hidden blessings, like 49 gates of galus followed by the fiftieth.

title.en: Faiths founded by one man

summary.en: Reviewing last year's emunah sessions on the Kuzari and the Rambam, the Rav contrasts Jewish emunah with other religions, each founded by one man whom people simply believed. He cites the Rambam, in a passage censored from Hilchos Melachim and in Igeres Teiman, that Christianity spread the idea of Mashiach, though a false one.

title.en: What multitudes witnessed cannot be denied

summary.en: The Rav states the rule that an event witnessed by multitudes and passed down cannot be denied. He illustrates it with Alexander the Great, Julius Caesar and George Washington, whose details may be doubted but not their existence, and with the Holocaust, which governments treat its denial as absurd.

title.en: Yetzias Mitzrayim and the written Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yetzias Mitzrayim spans the fifty days from Pesach to Shavuos and was seen by millions, as were the pillars of cloud and fire and the mann for forty years. At the end of the forty years Moshe Rabbeinu wrote Sifrei Torah for every shevet, and the people who had seen it all could confirm what was written; that same Torah is in every Jewish community today.

title.en: Matan Torah: a nation of prophets

summary.en: The Rav explains that the climax of the fifty days was Matan Torah, when every Jew became a navi and heard Hashem speak, something no other nation can claim. Hashem said this was so that the people would believe in Moshe forever; therefore Jews keep even milah because Moshe told them, not because of Avraham.

title.en: The survival of Klal Yisrael and Torah

summary.en: The Rav says wonders still happen if one pays attention, and that learning Jewish history shows how Klal Yisrael outlived every empire; he brings the Yaavetz that this survival is a greater miracle than the splitting of the sea. Unlike Greek and Roman culture, Torah is alive, and after the Holocaust it flourishes again, above all in Eretz Yisrael.

title.en: The Torah dares to promise

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the New Testament, which promises nothing except that Jews will never regain Yerushalayim, now its problem, with the Torah, which promises openly. The Torah promised that no one would covet the land while Jews went up three times a year, and it foretold where each shevet would settle, and both came true.

title.en: The promise of the sixth year

summary.en: The Rav turns to Shemitah, which begins in Elul, and the Torah's promise that the sixth year will yield enough for three years though the farmer may not work. He explains that the sixth year prepares for Shemitah, Shabbos of the land, as the sixth day prepares for Shabbos, and says this miracle is seen and documented today.

title.en: The Shemitah miracles of Komemiyus

summary.en: The Rav tells of Rav Binyamin Mendelson of Komemiyus: in the Shemitah of 5712 the neighbors' early planting rotted without rain while Komemiyus' old, wormy seed sown after Sukkos grew; in 5719 locusts devoured the surrounding fields and turned back at Komemiyus. He adds how the Jewish Agency's orchards in Komemiyus, left untended in Shemitah, flourished more than all others, as an official report records.

title.en: Shemitah today and the laws of nature

summary.en: The Rav notes that more farmers keep Shemitah each cycle and that this sixth year brought unusual rain after years of drought. He explains that the root of emunah is Har Sinai, yet Hashem does not show open miracles in every generation, because nature itself is a Torah Hashem wants kept, broken only at special times.

title.en: Shemitah as a lasting Har Sinai

summary.en: The Rav concludes that Shemitah in Eretz Yisrael defies nature like Matan Torah, but permanently, and this is one explanation of why Shemitah is tied to Har Sinai. He turns to Yovel, when every Jew returns to his portion, as an image of Mashiach, and blesses the listeners that Mashiach will point to them as those who brought him by staying faithful amid the street's impurity.

catalogTitle: בנקודה של זמן זוכים לנגוע בנקודה של “יחידה”

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that in the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, and above all at the close of Ne'ilah, every Jew can touch the level of yechidah, where all Jewish souls become one, and that this unity is the key to the geulah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Naval, who was given the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur to do teshuvah and wasted them. He explains the Chiddushei HaRim's saying that in these days the Avos knock on every Jewish heart: the spark inherited from the Avos is the root of the soul, and the ten days are the root of the year, so the two roots meet. He relates Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz's teaching that each Jew has a moment of yechidah in these days, and places it at the end of Ne'ilah, when all cry out 'Hashem echad'. Yechidah is where all souls merge, like Yaakov before the tribes divided, so hatred blocks it, and unity among Jews is needed for the geulah. Through the Midrash of the tailor's fish, the second luchos, Yom Kippur on Shabbos and Kol Nidrei, he develops these themes, ending with a plea that the ketz of 5748 not be spoiled by discord.

en: In the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah the Avos knock on every Jewish heart, because the spark inherited from them is the root of the soul and these ten days are the root of the whole year.
Every Jew has a moment in these days when he can reach yechidah, the highest level of the soul, and its climax is the cry of 'Hashem echad' at the end of Ne'ilah.
Yechidah is where all Jewish souls merge into one, as they were in Yaakov Avinu, so Yom Kippur is a day of achdus and hatred between Jews is a barrier to it.
The geulah depends on unity among Jews, and the Chasam Sofer said that a time fit for Mashiach was spoiled by the lashon hara and machlokes of its generation.
On Yom Kippur each Jew receives the second luchos, and the sealing at Ne'ilah is Hashem engraving them on his heart, giving him a heart for avodas Hashem for the whole year.
Yom Kippur is not a day without eating but a day of spiritual food, like the mann in its pure form, so a Jew who fasts properly also has oneg Shabbos when Yom Kippur falls on Shabbos.
Kol Nidrei is, according to the sefarim, an annulment of Hashem's oath to keep the Jews in galus.

title.en: Naval's ten days and the knocking of the Avos

summary.en: The Rav opens with David HaMelech's plea not to be made 'the shame of Naval', who was given the ten days of teshuvah and died. He brings the Chiddushei HaRim that in these days the Avos knock on every Jewish heart, and explains that each Jew carries an unquenchable spark inherited from Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov.

title.en: The ten days as the root of the year

summary.en: The Rav explains that as the Avos are the root of the soul, the ten days are the root of the year, so in them the Avos knock and Hashem is near. He describes the special holiness and light of these days and the Yom Kippur prayer in which Hashem calls to us, and returns to Naval, who ignored the shofar's call and slept on, which is why David prayed not to share his shame.

title.en: Rav Shraga Feivel's moment of yechidah

summary.en: The Rav recalls how Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz once spoke to the yeshivah in the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah about the five levels of the soul, saying each Jew has a moment of yechidah in these days and must wait for it and use it. The Rav adds that its climax is the end of Ne'ilah, when Jews cry 'Hashem echad'.

title.en: Yechidah, Yaakov Avinu and the day of 'echad'

summary.en: The Rav explains that at the level of yechidah all souls merge, like branches into the trunk of Yaakov Avinu, whose sons answered him with Shema Yisrael. Yom Kippur is the one day of the year that is 'echad', so it ends with Shema and Baruch Shem aloud, and for the same reason sins against a fellow Jew, hatred and anger, block a person from Yom Kippur.

title.en: Every Jew is in Haazinu

summary.en: The Rav brings the tradition that every Jew is alluded to in parshas Haazinu, and tells how the Satmar Rav, accused of hating Eretz Yisrael, answered with a smile with the closing words of the parshah. He explains that Haazinu, usually read the Shabbos before Yom Kippur, is the one parshah that holds all Jews together.

title.en: Achdus and the spoiled time of geulah

summary.en: The Rav says the geulah can only come through achdus, and one must pray much for unity among Jews and talmidei chachamim, as in the tefillah that all become one band. He brings the Chasam Sofer's word that the generation of Rav Yonasan Eybeschutz, the Pnei Yehoshua and Rav Yaakov Emden was fit for Mashiach, but the lashon hara around their machlokes spoiled it.

title.en: The tailor's fish on Erev Yom Kippur

summary.en: The Rav asks why Erev Yom Kippur has a festive meal and tells the Midrash of the Jewish tailor who outbid the governor's servant for the last fish, explaining that he rejoices that Hashem forgives sins, and later found a precious stone inside it. The Rav explains that the jewel stands for the seven blessings of the Yom Kippur Shemoneh Esrei that he merited to daven well.

title.en: Fish, Yonah and the tailor who joins pieces

summary.en: The Rav explains why fish are eaten on Shabbos: fish were not corrupted before the Mabul and are 'tzaddikim', so eating them brings sparks of righteousness. This links to Mincha of Yom Kippur, with the reading of arayos and the haftarah of Yonah praying inside the fish, and to the custom of buying Maftir Yonah for wealth, which he explains as true spiritual riches. A tailor joins torn pieces into one garment, an image of the achdus of Yom Kippur.

title.en: The second luchos engraved on the heart

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Yom Kippur is the day the second luchos were given, and the passuk 'write them on the tablet of your heart', explaining that the sealing at Ne'ilah is Hashem engraving the luchos on each heart according to how soft it has become. The true blessing is a heart for avodas Hashem all year, so the main request is for the neshamah, as the Yismach Moshe reads 'for Your sake, living G-d'.

title.en: Yom Kippur on Shabbos: fasting as oneg

summary.en: Since Yom Kippur falls on Shabbos that year, the Rav asks how one keeps oneg Shabbos while fasting, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar on 'if Israel kept two Shabbosos'. He answers that on Yom Kippur one eats spiritual food, the mann in its pure angelic form, so a true Jew finds his oneg in the fast itself, and Yom Kippur is the neshamah of the year.

title.en: Kol Nidrei: annulling the oath of galus

summary.en: The Rav asks why Yom Kippur opens with the annulment of vows, of all mitzvos. He brings the Gemara of Rabbah bar bar Chana, who heard a heavenly voice regret an oath and did not annul it, thinking it meant the oath of the Mabul when it meant the oath of galus, and explains that Kol Nidrei is an attempt to annul Hashem's oath of galus.

title.en: The ketz of 5748 and a plea for unity

summary.en: The Rav says tzaddikim long ago named 5748 as a time for Mashiach, notes that earlier dates passed without it and that a ketz not realized can turn harsh, and dismisses the state founded in an earlier such year as a worthless imitation. He closes with a plea that the year not be spoiled, that there be achdus among Jews and talmidei chachamim without lashon hara, and a brachah for a year of geulah.

catalogTitle: תשובה - הנשמה ישוב אל שורשה - הקב"ה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that yovel means returning to one's root, that teshuvah on Yom Kippur is the soul's return to the Kisei HaKavod, and that the year after shemittah carries the hope of the great shofar of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Shofros of Rosh Hashanah: the Torah was given with a shofar on the fiftieth day, a day above the seven-times-seven of nature. The Hebrew servant who refuses to go free at seven goes out at yovel. Yovel, he explains, means returning to the root, a law built into creation; the soul is hewn from the Kisei HaKavod, and teshuvah brings it back there. Rosh Hashanah is a day of judgment, the teruah of breaking, while Yom Kippur of yovel is the tekiah of mercy. Yovel applies only when all Jews dwell in the land, since its root is the place where all souls are one; so Yom Kippur demands reconciliation between Jews. Through the Maharal's idea of the eighth day above nature, he explains Yom Kippur as a second giving of the Torah, melaveh malkah as David HaMelech's meal, and Moshiach coming after shemittah. He closes that this Tishrei, after shemittah, is a special eis ratzon.

en: The Torah was given with a shofar on the fiftieth day, which is above the seven-times-seven order of the natural world.
Yovel means returning to the root, a general law of creation, and teshuvah is the soul's return to the Kisei HaKavod from which it was hewn.
Rosh Hashanah is a day of judgment whose teruah breaks; the tekiah of mercy comes from the yovel of Yom Kippur.
Yovel applies only when all of Israel dwell in the land, because it is the return to the root where all Jewish souls are joined; hence Yom Kippur requires Jews to be reconciled with each other.
Yom Kippur is the day the second luchos were given, a renewed matan Torah on a 'fiftieth day' after the sin of the golden calf.
The time after Shabbos and the year after shemittah hold the possibility of the 'eighth day' of Moshiach, which is why melaveh malkah is David HaMelech's meal.
This Tishrei after shemittah is like the 'shalosh seudos' of shemittah, a great eis ratzon when prayers are accepted.

title.en: The shofar of Sinai and the freed servant

summary.en: Starting from the Shofros of Rosh Hashanah, the Rav explains that the Torah, given with a shofar on the fiftieth day, comes from above the world. He brings the Hebrew servant who refuses freedom at seven but goes free at yovel, and Rav Tzadok's words that at the shofar of Moshiach even the lost will come running.

title.en: Yovel means returning to the root

summary.en: The Rav asks what yovel is, and explains from the Maharal, Koheles and the Ramban that everything in creation must return to its root. The Jewish soul comes from the Kisei HaKavod, and teshuvah, which reaches the Kisei HaKavod, returns it there.

title.en: The fiftieth day, the shofar and the shofar gadol

summary.en: The Rav explains that the soul and the Torah both come from above the seven-fold order of nature, from the fiftieth day. The shofar of Rosh Hashanah reminds a Jew where he comes from, but it is a small shofar; the great shofar of Moshiach is the true yovel, and the Torah's yovel shofar is blown on Yom Kippur.

title.en: Teruah of judgment, tekiah of mercy

summary.en: The Rav contrasts Rosh Hashanah, a day of din whose teruah means breaking, with Yom Kippur, a day of mercy. The Torah's verse for Rosh Hashanah mentions neither shofar nor tekiah, which are learned from the yovel of Yom Kippur. He brings the Baal HaTanya's Siddur that the tekiah after Yom Kippur is a higher one, an awakening of the shofar gadol.

title.en: Kol Yisrael: yovel needs all Jews together

summary.en: From the Noam Elimelech the Rav explains the root called 'Kol Yisrael', where all souls are joined. This is why yovel applies only when all Jews are in the land, and why Yom Kippur, itself a yovel, requires Jews to make peace with each other; he brings the Chasam Sofer that without appeasing one's fellow there is no atonement even between man and Hashem.

title.en: The eighth day above nature and the second luchos

summary.en: Yom Kippur includes all the days of the year, so it calls for a mitzvah that includes all mitzvos, loving one's fellow. The Rav brings the Maharal that the eighth is above nature, as with milah, Chanukah and the fiftieth day of Shavuos, and explains Yom Kippur as the day of the second luchos, a renewed matan Torah after the golden calf.

title.en: David HaMelech's prayer and David HaMelech's meal

summary.en: The Rav brings that besides the three tefillos of the Avos there is a fourth, tikkun chatzos, instituted by David HaMelech, and likewise a fourth meal, melaveh malkah. He asks why the meal of David, greatest of all, comes after Shabbos, and brings the Noam Megadim and the Gemara that Moshiach comes after shemittah.

title.en: The eighth day of Moshiach and motzaei Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav explains that when Moshiach comes the 'eighth day' will descend, with an eight-stringed harp and a day that is entirely Shabbos. At the end of every Shabbos and every shemittah there is a potential for this, so on motzaei Shabbos one eats David HaMelech's meal and sings of Eliyahu and Moshiach, and he brings the Midrash of the future feast where David says 'kos yeshuos esa'.

title.en: This Tishrei after shemittah: an eis ratzon

summary.en: The Rav says the coming Yom Kippur is a yovel-like Yom Kippur because it falls after shemittah, the time of hakhel, which he calls the 'shalosh seudos' of shemittah and an eis ratzon. He brings the Rambam that at hakhel one listens to the king's reading as if receiving the Torah at Sinai, and closes with a call to return to the root and a brachah for the geulah.

catalogTitle: The Significance of the 176 פסוקים in the פרשה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Naso, Tehillim 119 and Bava Basra each have 176 units, eight times the twenty-two letters, because Torah belongs to the number eight, above nature, and he links this to the Nazir, Shimshon and Mashiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the observation that Naso, the longest parsha, Tehillim 119, the longest psalm, and Bava Basra, the longest tractate, all have 176. He explains that seven is the number of nature and eight the number of what is above nature: the days of Mashiach, the eighth week after the Omer that extends Shavuos, Chanukah and its oil, the Kohen Gadol, and milah on the eighth day. The Torah, given at the start of the eighth week, belongs to eight, so Tehillim 119 repeats the alphabet eight times and Tehillim 19 turns to Torah in its eighth verse. Since the Torah has twenty-two letters, eight times twenty-two gives 176. He shows that Torah and Shavuos stand above space and time, then makes the Nazir the main theme of the parsha: Shimshon, a Nazir from birth, carried the potential of Mashiach, who will bring back the Jews who are cut off like hair. He closes with the hope that this year, 5748, Mashiach will come.

en: Seven is the number of nature and of the created world; eight is the number of what stands above nature.
The week after Shavuos is an eighth week, still an extension of Shavuos, in which one can still bring the festival offering and complete what was missed.
The Torah belongs to the number eight, so it was given at the start of the eighth week, and the parsha read in that week has eight times the twenty-two letters, 176 pesukim.
The Nazir, who separates himself from wine and the pleasures of this world, is the main theme of Naso, as the haftarah about Shimshon shows.
Shimshon, a Nazir from birth, had the makings of Mashiach, and Yaakov Avinu saw in him Mashiach; the generation did not merit it.
Mashiach will bring back the Jews who are cut off like hair and make them the crown of the whole structure of Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Why 176, and the meaning of eight

summary.en: The Rav notes that Naso, Tehillim 119 and Bava Basra, each the longest of its kind, all have 176, and asks why. He explains that seven is the number of nature and eight what is above it, and that the eighth year, after Shemitah, is fit for Mashiach.

title.en: The eighth week extends Shavuos

summary.en: The Rav explains from the Gemara that after counting seven weeks the following eighth week is an extension of the one-day Yom Tov of Shavuos, when the festival offering can still be brought. A person who did not use Shavuos for his na'aseh venishma can still do so in this week.

title.en: Wine for Shabbos, oil for Chanukah

summary.en: The Rav contrasts wine, yayin, whose gematria is seventy and with which Shabbos, the seventh day, is sanctified, with olive oil, shemen, which shares its letters with shemonah, eight, and sanctifies the eight days of Chanukah. Following the Maharal, Chanukah's days are borrowed from the days of Mashiach, its miracle came through the Kohen Gadol, and he wears eight garments.

title.en: Milah, the seventy nations, and Torah

summary.en: The Rav explains with the Maharal that milah is on the eighth day because removing the orlah defies nature. The seventy nations belong to seven, Klal Yisrael to eight, and the Torah, which separates Jews from the nations, was given at the start of the eighth week.

title.en: Tehillim 119 and Tehillim 19

summary.en: The Rav shows that Tehillim 119, a prayer about Torah, goes through the alef-beis eight times, as the Maharal explains, because Torah belongs to eight. Likewise Tehillim 19 speaks of nature for seven verses and turns to Torah in the eighth; he then returns to Naso, read in the eighth week.

title.en: Eight times twenty-two is 176

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Torah's letters come from twenty-two roots, so Naso, belonging to Shavuos and the eighth week, has eight times twenty-two pesukim, and Bava Basra has 176 daf counting the unwritten first daf. He adds that the last 89 pesukim of Naso are the Chanukah reading, and 89 is the gematria of Chanukah.

title.en: Above space and above time

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the Aron in the Kodesh HaKodashim took up no space, because Torah is above the laws of nature. Shavuos, defined by the count rather than a date, and Zos Chanukah are likewise not fixed to the calendar, and both fall in the third month of their half of the year.

title.en: The Nazir, the main theme of Naso

summary.en: The Rav lists the three laws of the Nazir: no wine, no cutting the hair, no contact with the dead. From the haftarah about Shimshon he shows that the Nazir is the parsha's main theme, and explains that wine stands for the intoxication of a world chasing pleasure, while the Nazir is sober and wears a crown, nezer.

title.en: Shimshon, head of all Nezirim

summary.en: The Rav explains that each virtue has a tzaddik at its head: Moshe Rabbeinu for those who toil in Torah, Dovid HaMelech for those who daven, and Shimshon for every Nazir. Unlike an ordinary Nazir, who takes a vow for thirty days, Shimshon was a Nazir from birth, as the angel told his mother.

title.en: Klal Yisrael as one body, and its hair

summary.en: After briefly recalling Shimshon's strength and his end, the Rav explains that all of Klal Yisrael is one structure, like Adam HaRishon whose limbs held different souls: the wise are the head, givers of tzedakah the hands, those who daven the heart. Hair, which lives on even after death, stands for Jews who are cut off and lifeless, whom Mashiach, who belongs to the world of eight, will restore.

title.en: Yaakov saw Shimshon as Mashiach

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Nazir's holiness lies in his hair and that Shimshon is an aspect of Mashiach. He brings the Midrash on Yaakov's blessing to Dan: Yaakov saw Shimshon's strength and thought he was Mashiach, then saw him killed and said 'I hope for Your salvation'. Yaakov was not mistaken; Shimshon could have been Mashiach had the generation merited it.

title.en: The year 5748, and the crown of the Nazir

summary.en: The Rav says tzaddikim taught that this year, 5748, has great potential for Mashiach, and hints at it through the Sotah's 'amen amen' in the parsha. He explains that when Mashiach comes the cut-off hair will be restored as the crown of the structure, the ba'alei teshuvah, and that Shimshon came from the tribe of Dan, itself cut off from the clouds of glory, to restore it.

title.en: The lion, the gates of Azah, and the call to act

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shimshon tore apart a lion, the mazal of Av, the month of the Churban, and tore out the city gates that held him, showing what Mashiach will do to the barriers before every Jew. He closes that this year has great potential, that one still believes even if Mashiach tarries, and that in this eighth week each person should contribute what he can to become a good Jew.
